Archbold - Polygala lewtonii - Summary

Authors: Niklas Neisse (neisse.n@protonmail.com), Aspen Workman, Aldo Compagnoni (aldo.compagnoni@idiv.de)

1 Introduction

The supplementary material to the Polygala lewtonii dataset from Archbold Biological Station.

The GIS and Data Management program at Archbold Biological Station maintains a comprehensive collection of ecological and environmental data gathered through various research initiatives and ongoing long-term monitoring projects. One key platform for accessing this data is the Archbold Biological Station’ Ecological Data Inventory (EDI), which hosts extensive datasets related to biodiversity, land cover, climate, and ecological patterns.

For our model, we utilized 16 years of demographic data on short-lived herb endemic to fire-maintained Florida sandhills - Polygala lewtonii using an Integrated Population Model (IPM). This dataset has previously been used in the work of Weekley and Menges, 2012.

1.1 Setup

We use the following packages: tidyverse, patchwork, skimr, ipmr, binom, bbmle, gridExtra, lme4

2 Data

This dataset documents the long-term demographic monitoring of 5,060 individually marked Polygala lewtonii (Lewton’s milkwort) plants at the Lake Wales Ridge National Wildlife Refuge, Carter Creek, in south-central Florida. From December 2001 to December 2017—and continuing beyond—data were collected quarterly from 220 permanent 25 cm-radius circular plots across six management units in yellow sandhill habitat.

Each plant was marked with a uniquely coded plastic toothpick and flag, and its spatial position within the plot was recorded by angle and distance from the center. Survival and recruitment were recorded four times per year (March, June, September, December), while detailed measurements of size (height, crown diameter, number of stems) and reproductive effort (flowering stem count) were collected each March. Due to the amphicarphic nature of P. lewtonii, only aboveground (chasmogamous) flower data were recorded.

The site experienced four prescribed fires (2001, 2007, 2009, 2015). Post-fire observations included plant-level fire exposure (e.g., singed, scorched, consumed) and percent area burned per plot (except for the 2001 fire). The dataset captures both mortality and recruitment following fire, contributing to an understanding of population responses to disturbance. Importantly, the species does not exhibit dormancy, and plants marked as dead were rarely observed alive in subsequent censuses.

2.1 Tails from meta

“Plants were censused during their peak of reproduction annually in July and August”

“In 220 permanent 25 cm radius circular plots, plants were marked with plastic toothpick”

“Data collection occurred quarterly with survival and recruitment recorded in March, June, September and December and more detailed measures of size and fecundity taken in March”

“This species is amphicarphic with both showy-open flowers produced in spring (chasmogamy) and closed, self-pollinating flowers both above- and belowground produced in late summer (cleistogamy). Therefore, our fecundity data are based only on chasmogamy.”

“This dataset also captures post-fire mortality and recruitment events following four prescribed burns.”

“Plants that had died were given a ‘dead’ code (0) indicating first time dead but toothpicks and marking flags remained in the field. At the next census, if the plant was still dead, it was given a ‘previously dead’ code (9) and the toothpick and marking flag were removed from the field.”

“Plant dormancy does not occur in this species and very few individuals marked as dead were alive in the subsequent census.”

“In March, we took additional size measures”

“four prescribed burns during the 2001-2017 study, although not all plots were affected”

“status of the plant as unburned, singed (some green), scorched (no green but brown leaves remained), or consumed (little to no plant material remained).”

“P. lewtonii plants are usually killed by fire and seedlings recruit post-fire from a soil seedbank (B. Pace-Aldana, pers. comm.; C. W. Weekley, unpubl. data).”

“A separate field experiment demonstrated that buried seeds may retain viability for at least 2 years (C. W. Weekley and E. S. Menges, unpubl. data), indicating that P. lewtonii is capable of accumulating a persistent (sensuThompson and Grime 1979) soil seedbank. The sudden appearance of large cohorts of seedling recruits suggests that the persistent seedbanks of P. lewtonii are ecologically relevant.”

“In the March 2002 census, burned quadrats out-recruited unburned quadrats 3.7–1 (184.0% v. 49.2%; c2 = 48.880, d.f. = 1, P < 0.001). Over the 2 censuses, burned quadrats had proportional recruitment of between 75.8% and 79.0% of seedlings recruited into burned quadrats with no surviving reproductive adults, indicating that most recruitment was from the preburn seedbank rather than from newly produced seeds.”

2.3 Data exploration

From the data portal we get two datasets. The first data set contains information about burn status across various quadrants over time. It includes columns for the date, unit number, quadrant identifier, burn status (likely indicating whether a burn event occurred), and the percentage of the area burned. The data spans different dates and quadrants, showing no burn events (burn_status = 0) and mostly zero or NA values for percentage burned, indicating areas that were unburned or had no available data on burning.

The second dataset consists of 196,099 records documenting the life histories of Polygala lewtonii individuals monitored quarterly from 2001 to 2017 across 220 fixed circular plots. Each plant was uniquely located within a plot using a combination of its spatial position (plot unit, quadrat, angle, and distance from plot center), and observed repeatedly through time. For each census, field staff recorded whether the plant was alive, newly dead, or previously dead (plant status), its developmental stage (seedling, juvenile, or adult), structural size (plant height, crown spread, number of stems), and reproductive output (number of flowering stems). Additionally, some plants were flagged as post-fire recruits if they appeared following one of four prescribed burns conducted during the study period.

Initial exploration revealed inconsistencies in plant identification across time. Plant IDs were sometimes reused, with different individuals appearing under the same identifier in different years, occasionally with different spatial coordinates. To resolve this, we redefined plant identity to include both its original tag and its spatial position within the plot, allowing us to track unique individuals throughout the study.

We also identified duplicated entries for the same plant and census period, some with conflicting information about size or status. These duplicates were reviewed and filtered out when necessary. A small number of records had a status code indicating the plant could not be relocated; these were removed due to their ambiguity. Another subset of plants entered the dataset with an undefined status code not described in the field protocol; based on their behavior in subsequent years, we reclassified these as living individuals rather than new recruits.

Several individuals marked as new recruits were never measured for size and died within the same census interval. These contributed no usable demographic information and were excluded to avoid inflating recruitment or mortality rates. For the remaining plants, we reconstructed continuous life histories by ordering observations over time and linking size measurements across consecutive censuses to estimate individual growth trajectories. We calculated derived variables such as above-ground volume (from crown diameter and height) and next-step size values to enable later demographic modeling.

Fire exposure was inconsistently recorded, but we inferred post-fire recruitment by marking individuals that appeared shortly after known burn events. When fire status was missing within a year, we carried forward the highest fire exposure level reported for any individual within that group.

The final processed dataset contains consistently tracked individuals with complete life histories, including identity, spatial location, observation date, survival status, plant developmental stage, structural size, reproductive effort, and fire exposure history. This curated dataset forms a reliable basis for examining how individual-level traits and disturbance history influence population-level dynamics over space and time.

Code 
df <- df_og %>% 
  separate(col = date, into = c('year', 'month'), sep = '-') %>% 
  mutate(id = paste0(unit, '_', quad, '_', id, '_', angle, '-', dist)) %>% 
  arrange(unit, id, year, month) %>% #view()
  # Month of death
  group_by(id) %>%
  mutate(death = paste0(year, "_", month)[which(survival == 0)[1]]) %>%
  ungroup() %>% #view()
  # Code 2 survival: individual not found, 5 in total. REMOVE
  filter(!id %in% (df_og %>% 
                     mutate(id = paste0(unit, '_', quad, '_', id, '_', angle, '-', dist)) %>%
                     filter(survival == 2) %>% 
                     pull(id) %>% 
                     unique())) %>% #view()
# Fire: For now we will just drag the maximum value of each year with us
  dplyr::select(!c(angle, dist)) %>% #view()
  group_by(id, year) %>%
  mutate(postburn_plant = if_else(all(is.na(postburn_plant)), NA_real_,
                                  max(postburn_plant, na.rm = TRUE))) %>%
  ungroup() %>% #view()
  filter(survival < 9) %>% 
  # Recruits: 5 indicates that the plant was detected for the first time. 
  #  however, there are plants that were detected in a month without size measurement
  #  many of them are present in the next year too.. for now I will count them as recruits too
  #  actually I can give them a 2 - I like it, easy to change later too..
  # Furthermore, 1_609_101_100-19 is an example of how it is not considered a recruit in the original data set
  #  if the plant was there already in the fist year of the sampling campaign (i.e. 2001)
  #  We also don't know if it was or wasn't a recruit and thus it gets an NA
  group_by(id) %>%
  mutate(
    recruit = if_else(
      (lag(survival) == 5 & is.na(lag(stage))), 2, 0, missing = 0)) %>% 
  mutate(recruit = if_else(survival == 5, 1, recruit)) %>% 
  mutate(recruit = if_else(as.numeric(year) == 2001, NA_real_, recruit)) %>% 
  mutate(recruit = if_else(stage == 1, 1, recruit)) %>% 
  ungroup() %>% #view()
  # Survival: 
  #  Since there is no dormancy I can remove everything that does not have a size 
  filter(!is.na(stage)) %>% #view()
  group_by(id) %>%
  mutate(
    survival = if_else(row_number() == n(), 0, survival)) %>%
  ungroup() %>% #view()
  # Include the NEW ADDITIONS (survival == 3)
  mutate(survival = if_else(survival == 3, 1, survival),
         survival = if_else(survival == 5, 1, survival)) %>% 
  # Growth:
  group_by(id) %>%
  mutate(size_t1   = lead(height),
         c_dim_t1  = lead(crown_diameter),
         stems_t1  = lead(stems),
         volume_t0 = ((crown_diameter / 2) ^ 2) * pi * height,
         volume_t1 = lead(volume_t0)) %>%
  ungroup()%>% 
  rename(survives = survival,
         size_t0  = height,
         site     = unit) %>% 
  mutate(logsize_t0   = log(size_t0),
         logsize_t1   = log(size_t1),    
         logsize_t0_2 = logsize_t0^2,     
         logsize_t0_3 = logsize_t0^3,
         logvol_t0    = log(volume_t0),
         logvol_t1    = log(volume_t1),
         logvol_t0_2  = logvol_t0^2,
         logvol_t0_3  = logvol_t0^3,
         year         = as.numeric(year),
         stage        = as.factor( stage),
         recruits     = if_else(recruit > 0, 1, recruit),
         flower       = if_else(stage == 3, 1, 0)) %>%
  dplyr::select(site, quad, cohort, id, year, 
         stage, survives, size_t0, flower, flowering_stems, recruits, recruit, 
         size_t1, logsize_t1, logsize_t0, logsize_t0_2, logsize_t0_3,
         crown_diameter, stems, postburn_plant,
         volume_t0, volume_t1, logvol_t0, logvol_t1, logvol_t0_2, logvol_t0_3)

3 Investigations

Code 
library(MASS)

3.1 Seedbank

There is no information on seed banks in the meta data, nor in the original data.

The published literature and associated unpublished data strongly suggest that Polygala lewtonii relies on a persistent soil seedbank for post-fire recruitment. While the dataset itself contains no direct information on seed banks, several observations and experimental results provide compelling indirect evidence for their ecological importance.

Field observations indicate that most post-fire recruits emerged in quadrats where no surviving reproductive adults were present, implying that recruitment originated from seeds deposited in earlier years. Specifically, the study notes that:

‘For these 2 cohorts, between 75.8% and 79.0% of seedlings recruited into burned quadrats with no surviving reproductive adults, indicating that most recruitment was from the preburn seedbank rather than from newly produced seeds.’

The timing of recruitment relative to fire and flowering supports this conclusion:

‘Recruits in the first 2 post-burn cohorts (December 2001 and March 2002) came from the seedbank, rather than from seeds shed by surviving adults, which did not produce chasmogamous flowers between the August 2001 burn and the December 2001 and March 2002 censuses.’

Supporting this field evidence, a separate experiment demonstrated long-term seed viability:

‘A separate field experiment demonstrated that buried seeds may retain viability for at least 2 years (C. W. Weekley and E. S. Menges, unpubl. data), indicating that P. lewtonii is capable of accumulating a persistent (sensu Thompson and Grime 1979) soil seedbank.’

The study also suggests that fire enhances the reproductive success of recruits, reinforcing the seedbank’s role in population dynamics:

‘The combined effects of higher seedling recruitment, higher survival to reproduction and earlier flowering indicate that P. lewtonii plants recruiting into burned microsites make a greater contribution to the seedbank, and thus to the long-term viability of the population, than do recruits in unburned microsites.’

While smoke-stimulated germination has been demonstrated in the lab, field evidence is limited: However in their publication they do not specify any germination rates (Lindon and Menges, 2008).

‘In a laboratory experiment, Lindon and Menges (2008) showed that short-term exposure to smoke promoted ex situ germination in P. lewtonii, but this result was not supported by a field experiment (C.W. Weekley, unpubl. data).’

Overall, although the dataset itself does not directly record seedbank dynamics, the documented timing of recruitment, absence of flowering adults, and experimental findings together indicate that P. lewtonii maintains a persistent and ecologically meaningful soil seedbank that plays a key role in its post-fire recovery and long-term persistence.

3.2 Fire

The site experienced four prescribed fires (2001, 2007, 2009, 2015). Post-fire observations included plant-level fire exposure (e.g., singed, scorched, consumed) and percent area burned per plot (except for the 2001 fire). The dataset captures both mortality and recruitment following fire, contributing to an understanding of population responses to disturbance. Importantly, the species does not exhibit dormancy, and plants marked as dead were rarely observed alive in subsequent censuses.

‘This dataset also captures post-fire mortality and recruitment events following four prescribed burns.’ ‘[…] four prescribed burns during the 2001-2017 study, although not all plots were affected’ ‘P. lewtonii plants are usually killed by fire and seedlings recruit post-fire from a soil seedbank (B. Pace-Aldana, pers. comm.; C. W. Weekley, unpubl. data).’

3.2.1 The extent of fire

To assess whether visual signs of fire damage on individual plants persist beyond the year of fire, we examined the variable postburn_plant, which records damage severity following prescribed burns. Specifically, we tested whether plants showing fire damage in one year continued to exhibit signs of fire in the subsequent year. Despite repeated prescribed burns in 2001, 2007, 2009, and 2015, our analysis found no evidence that fire damage carries over across years at the individual level. That is, plants recorded as damaged in one year were not marked as damaged again in the following year. This suggests that visible fire effects are either short-lived or not consistently recorded beyond the fire year.

Code 
df %>%
  filter(!is.na(postburn_plant)) %>%
  mutate(fire = if_else(postburn_plant > 0, TRUE, FALSE)) %>%
  arrange(id, year) %>%
  group_by(id) %>%
  mutate(
    fire_t = fire,
    fire_t1 = lead(fire),       
    year_t1 = lead(year)) %>%
  filter(year_t1 == year + 1) %>% 
  ungroup()

## #   logvol_t0_3 <dbl>, fire <lgl>, fire_t <lgl>, fire_t1 <lgl>, year_t1 <dbl>

To quantify fire severity across space and time, we calculated the proportion of individuals with visible signs of fire damage (postburn_plant > 0) in each plot-year. Only plot-years with at least one scorched individual were included. This metric reflects within-plot fire intensity as experienced by the plant population.

Code 
df %>%
  filter(!is.na(postburn_plant)) %>%
  mutate(fire = postburn_plant > 0) %>%
  group_by(site, quad, year) %>%
  summarise(
    n_total = n(),
    n_fire = sum(fire),
    severity = n_fire / n_total,
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  filter(n_fire > 0)

To better understand the temporal patterns of fire effects on individual plants, we summarized the presence of fire damage signs (postburn_plant > 0) across months and years. By grouping observations by year and month, we quantified both the number and proportion of individuals exhibiting scorch damage.

Code 
df_og %>%
  separate(col = date, into = c("year", "month"), sep = "-") %>%
  filter(!is.na(postburn_plant)) %>%
  mutate(fire = postburn_plant > 0) %>%
  group_by(year, month) %>%
  summarise(
    n_total = n(),
    n_fire = sum(fire),
    pct_fire = round(100 * n_fire / n_total, 1),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  arrange(year, month)

Code 
# Logistic regression
mod_su_0 <- glm(survives ~ fire,
                data = df_su, family = 'binomial') 
# Logistic regression
mod_su_1 <- glm(survives ~ logvol_t0 + fire,
                data = df_su, family = 'binomial') 
# Quadratic logistic model
mod_su_2 <- glm(survives ~ logvol_t0 + logvol_t0_2 + fire,
                data = df_su, family = 'binomial')  
# Cubic logistic model
mod_su_3 <- glm(survives ~ logvol_t0 + logvol_t0_2 + logvol_t0_3 + fire,
                data = df_su, family = 'binomial')  


# Compare models using AIC
mods_su      <- list(mod_su_0, mod_su_1, mod_su_2, mod_su_3)
mods_su_dAIC <- AICtab(mods_su, weights = T, sort = F)$dAIC

# Get the sorted indices of dAIC values
mods_su_sorted <- order(mods_su_dAIC)

# Establish the index of model complexity
if (length(v_mod_set_su) == 0) {
  mod_su_index_bestfit <- mods_su_sorted[1]
  v_mod_su_index       <- mod_su_index_bestfit - 1 
} else {
  mod_su_index_bestfit <- v_mod_set_su +1
  v_mod_su_index       <- v_mod_set_su}

mod_su_bestfit <- mods_su[[mod_su_index_bestfit]]
mod_su_ranef   <- coef(mod_su_bestfit)

# Create prediction data frames for fire = 0 and fire = 1
df_su_pred <- data.frame(
  logvol_t0 = rep(seq(min(na.omit(df_su$logvol_t0)), 
                      max(na.omit(df_su$logvol_t0)), length.out = 100), 2),
  fire = rep(c(FALSE, TRUE), each = 100)) %>% 
  mutate(logvol_t0_2 = logvol_t0^2,
         fire_label = ifelse(fire == 1, 'Fire', 'No fire')) %>% 
  mutate(survives = predict(mod_su_bestfit, newdata = ., type = 'response'))

# Binned observed data for both fire levels
df_su_binned <- bind_rows(
  plot_binned_prop(filter(df_su, fire == 0), 10, logvol_t0, survives) %>%
    mutate(fire_label = 'No fire'),
  plot_binned_prop(filter(df_su, fire == 1), 10, logvol_t0, survives) %>%
    mutate(fire_label = 'Fire'))

# Plot 1: Raw data + prediction lines
fig_su_line_combined <- ggplot() +
  geom_jitter(data = df_su, aes(x = logvol_t0, y = survives, color = fire_label),
              alpha = 0.25, width = 0.08, height = 0.3) +
  geom_line(data = df_su_pred, aes(x = logvol_t0, y = survives, color = fire_label),
            linewidth = 0.9) +  
  scale_color_manual(values = c('No fire' = 'black', 'Fire' = 'red')) +
  theme_bw() +
  labs(title = NULL, x = 'Volume at time t0 (log)', y = 'Survival to time t1') +
  theme(legend.position = 'none')

# Plot 2: Binned proportions + prediction lines
fig_su_bin_combined <- ggplot() +
  geom_point(data = df_su_binned, aes(x = logvol_t0, y = survives, color = fire_label)) +
  geom_errorbar(data = df_su_binned, aes(x = logvol_t0, ymin = lwr, ymax = upr, color = fire_label),
                width = 0.2) +
  geom_line(data = df_su_pred, aes(x = logvol_t0, y = survives, color = fire_label),
            linewidth = 0.9) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c('No fire' = 'black', 'Fire' = 'red')) +
  theme_bw() +
  ylim(0, 1) +
  labs(title = NULL, x = 'Volume at time t0 (log)', y = 'Survival to time t1', 
       color = 'At time t0') +
  theme(legend.position = 'top')

# Combine the two plots
fig_su_all <- fig_su_line_combined + fig_su_bin_combined +
  plot_annotation(
    title = 'Survival',
    subtitle = v_ggp_suffix,
    theme = theme(

      plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 10, face = 'italic')))

  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = lwr, ymax = upr), width = 0.2, linewidth = 0.5) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c('No fire' = 'black', 'Fire' = 'red')) +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = c(0.1, 0.5, 0.9), limits = c(0, 1.01)) +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(
    axis.text = element_text(size = 8),
    title = element_text(size = 10),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 8),
    legend.position = 'top') +
  labs(
    title    = 'Flowering probability by fire status',
    subtitle = v_ggp_suffix,
    x        = expression('Volume (log)'[t0]),
    y        = 'Flowering Probability\nat time t0',
    color    = 'At time t0')

fig_fl_overall

Code 
# Logistic regression
mod_fl_0 <- glm(flower ~ fire,
                data = df_fl, family = 'binomial') 
# Logistic regression
mod_fl_1 <- glm(flower ~ logvol_t0 + fire,
                data = df_fl, family = 'binomial') 
# Quadratic logistic model
mod_fl_2 <- glm(flower ~ logvol_t0 + logvol_t0_2 + fire,
                data = df_fl, family = 'binomial')  
# Cubic logistic model
mod_fl_3 <- glm(flower ~ logvol_t0 + logvol_t0_2 + logvol_t0_3 + fire,
                data = df_fl, family = 'binomial')  

# Compare models using AIC
mods_fl      <- list(mod_fl_0, mod_fl_1, mod_fl_2, mod_fl_3)
mods_fl_dAIC <- AICtab(mods_fl, weights = T, sort = F)$dAIC

# Get the sorted indices of dAIC values
mods_fl_sorted <- order(mods_fl_dAIC)

# Establish the index of model complexity
if (length(v_mod_set_fl) == 0) {
  mod_fl_index_bestfit <- mods_fl_sorted[1]
  v_mod_fl_index       <- mod_fl_index_bestfit - 1 
} else {
  mod_fl_index_bestfit <- v_mod_set_fl +1
  v_mod_fl_index       <- v_mod_set_fl
  }

mod_fl_bestfit <- mods_fl[[mod_fl_index_bestfit]]
mod_fl_ranef   <- coef(mod_fl_bestfit)


# Add predictions using model
df_fl_pred <- data.frame(
  logvol_t0 = rep(seq(
    min(df_fl$logvol_t0, na.rm = TRUE), 
    max(df_fl$logvol_t0, na.rm = TRUE), length.out = 100), 2),
  fire = rep(c(F, T), each = 100)) %>%
  mutate(
    fire_label = ifelse(fire == 1, 'Fire', 'No fire'),
    logvol_t0_2 = logvol_t0^2,
    logvol_t0_3 = logvol_t0^3) %>% 
  mutate(flower = predict(mod_fl_bestfit, newdata = ., type = 'response'))

# Binned observed data for both fire levels
df_fl_binned <- bind_rows(
  plot_binned_prop(filter(df_fl, fire == 0), 10, logvol_t0, flower) %>%
    mutate(fire_label = 'No fire'),
  plot_binned_prop(filter(df_fl, fire == 1), 10, logvol_t0, flower) %>%
    mutate(fire_label = 'Fire'))

# Plot 1: Raw jitter + prediction lines
fig_fl_line_combined <- ggplot() +
  geom_jitter(data = df_fl %>% filter(fire == 0), 
              aes(x = logvol_t0, y = flower, color = fire_label),
              alpha = 0.1, width = 0.08, height = 0.2) +
  geom_jitter(data = df_fl %>% filter(fire == 1), 
              aes(x = logvol_t0, y = flower, color = fire_label),
              alpha = 0.5, width = 0.08, height = 0.2) +
  geom_line(data = df_fl_pred, aes(x = logvol_t0, y = flower, color = fire_label),
            linewidth = 0.9) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c('No fire' = 'black', 'Fire' = 'red')) +
  theme_bw() +
  labs(title = NULL, x = 'Size at time t0 (log)', y = 'Flowering Probability') +
  theme(legend.position = 'none')

# Plot 2: Binned points + error bars + prediction lines
fig_fl_bin_combined <- ggplot() +
  geom_point(data = df_fl_binned, aes(x = logvol_t0, y = flower, color = fire_label)) +
  geom_errorbar(data = df_fl_binned, aes(x = logvol_t0, ymin = lwr, ymax = upr, color = fire_label),
                width = 0.2) +
  geom_line(data = df_fl_pred, aes(x = logvol_t0, y = flower, color = fire_label),
            linewidth = 0.9) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c('No fire' = 'black', 'Fire' = 'red')) +
  theme_bw() +
  ylim(0, 1) +
  labs(title = NULL, x = 'Size at time t0 (log)', y = 'Flowering Probability') +
  theme(legend.title = element_blank(), legend.position = 'top')

# Combine the two plots with patchwork
fig_fl_all <- fig_fl_line_combined + fig_fl_bin_combined +
  plot_annotation(
    title = 'Flowering',
    subtitle = v_ggp_suffix,
    theme = theme(
      plot.title = element_text(size = 14, face = 'bold'),
      plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 10, face = 'italic')))

df_fe <- df %>%
  mutate(fire = if_else(postburn_plant > 0 & !is.na(postburn_plant), T, F),
         fire_label = if_else(fire == 1, 'Fire', 'No fire')) %>% 
  filter(flower == 1, !is.na(logvol_t0)) %>%

Code 
mod_fe_0 <- glm.nb(flowering_stems ~ fire, data = df_fe)
mod_fe_1 <- glm.nb(flowering_stems ~ fire + logvol_t0, data = df_fe)
mod_fe_2 <- glm.nb(flowering_stems ~ fire + logvol_t0 + logvol_t0_2, data = df_fe)
mod_fe_3 <- glm.nb(flowering_stems ~ fire + logvol_t0 + logvol_t0_2 + logvol_t0_3, data = df_fe)

mods_fe      <- list(mod_fe_0, mod_fe_1, mod_fe_2, mod_fe_3)
mods_fe_dAIC <- AICctab(mods_fe, weights = T, sort = F)$dAIC
mods_fe_i_sort <- order(mods_fe_dAIC)

if (length(v_mod_set_fe) == 0) {
  mod_fe_i_best <- mods_fe_i_sort[1]
  v_mod_fe_i    <- mod_fe_i_best - 1 
} else {
  mod_fe_i_best <- v_mod_set_fe +1
  v_mod_fe_i    <- v_mod_set_fe
  }

mod_fe_best  <- mods_fe[[mod_fe_i_best]]
mod_fe_ranef <- coef(mod_fe_best)

df_fe_preddata <- tibble(
  logvol_t0 = rep(seq(min(df_fe$logvol_t0, na.rm = TRUE),
                  max(df_fe$logvol_t0, na.rm = TRUE),
                  length.out = 100), 2),
  fire       = rep(c(F, T), each = 100)) %>%
  mutate(logvol_t0_2 = logvol_t0^2,
         logvol_t0_3 = logvol_t0^3,
         fire_label  = ifelse(fire == 1, 'Fire', 'No fire'))

mod_fe_pred <- predict(mod_fe_best, newdata = df_fe_preddata, type = 'link', se.fit = TRUE)

df_fe_preddata <- df_fe_preddata %>%
  mutate(
    fit_link = mod_fe_pred$fit,
    se_link  = mod_fe_pred$se.fit,
    fit_link_lower = fit_link - 1.96 * se_link,
    fit_link_upper = fit_link + 1.96 * se_link,
    predicted_stems = exp(fit_link),
    predicted_stems_lower = exp(fit_link_lower),
    predicted_stems_upper = exp(fit_link_upper))

fig_fe <- ggplot(df_fe, aes(x = logvol_t0, y = flowering_stems, color = fire_label)) +
  geom_jitter(data = df_fe %>% filter(fire == F), 
              aes(x = logvol_t0, y = flowering_stems, color = fire_label),
              width = 0.1, height = 0.2, alpha = 0.1) +
  geom_jitter(data = df_fe %>% filter(fire == T), 
              aes(x = logvol_t0, y = flowering_stems, color = fire_label),
              width = 0.1, height = 0.2, alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_line(data = df_fe_preddata, 
            aes(x = logvol_t0, y = predicted_stems, color = fire_label), size = 1.2) +
  geom_ribbon(
    data = df_fe_preddata,
    aes(x = logvol_t0, ymin = predicted_stems_lower, ymax = predicted_stems_upper, fill = fire_label),
    alpha = 0.1, inherit.aes = FALSE) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c('No fire' = 'black', 'Fire' = 'red')) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c('No fire' = 'black', 'Fire' = 'red')) +
  labs(
    title    = 'Fecundity',
    subtitle = v_ggp_suffix,
    x        = 'Volume t0 (log)',
    y        = 'Number of Flowering Stems\nin time t0',
    color    = 'At time t0',
    fill     = 'At time t0') +

3.2.6 Fire on Recruitment transition

This analysis examines how the total number of flowering stems in year t influences recruitment in year t+1, and whether this relationship is affected by fire in the previous year.

Code 
df_fs2r <- df %>%
  group_by(site, quad, year) %>%
  mutate(fire = if_else(postburn_plant > 0 & !is.na(postburn_plant), T, F)) %>%
  summarise(
    total_stocks = sum(flowering_stems, na.rm = TRUE),
    fire = any(fire == T),
    .groups = 'drop') %>%
  full_join(df %>%
               group_by(site, quad, year) %>%
               summarise(
                 recruit_count_t1 = sum(recruits, na.rm = TRUE),
                 .groups = 'drop') %>%
               mutate(year = year - 1), 
             by = c('site', 'quad', 'year')) %>%
  mutate(fire_label = ifelse(fire, "Fire", "No Fire"))
  
mod_fs2r_01 <- glm.nb(recruit_count_t1 ~ fire, data = df_fs2r)
mod_fs2r_02 <- glm.nb(recruit_count_t1 ~ total_stocks + fire, data = df_fs2r)
mod_fs2r_11 <- glm.nb(recruit_count_t1 ~ total_stocks * fire, data = df_fs2r)

mods_fs2r      <- list(mod_fs2r_01,  mod_fs2r_02, mod_fs2r_11)
mods_fs2r_dAIC <- AICctab(mods_fs2r, weights = T, sort = F)$dAIC

# Plot: Effect of fire only (mod_fs2r_01)
df_fs2r_newdata <- data.frame(fire = c(FALSE, TRUE))
df_fs2r_newdata$fit <- predict(mod_fs2r_01, newdata = df_fs2r_newdata, type = 'response')
pred_link <- predict(mod_fs2r_01, newdata = df_fs2r_newdata, type = 'link', se.fit = TRUE)
df_fs2r_newdata$lower <- exp(pred_link$fit - 1.96 * pred_link$se.fit)
df_fs2r_newdata$upper <- exp(pred_link$fit + 1.96 * pred_link$se.fit)
df_fs2r_newdata$fire <- factor(df_fs2r_newdata$fire, levels = c(FALSE, TRUE), labels = c('No Fire', 'Fire'))

ggplot(df_fs2r_newdata, aes(x = fire, y = fit, fill = fire)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.6, color = 'gray30') +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = lower, ymax = upper), width = 0.2, color = 'gray30') +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c('No Fire' = '#1b9e77', 'Fire' = '#d95f02')) + 
  labs(
    x = 'Fire in Previous Year',
    y = 'Predicted Recruitment Count (t+1)',
    title = 'Effect of Fire on Recruitment') +
  theme_bw(base_size = 14) +
  theme(legend.position = 'none')

Code 
# Plot: Effect of total_stocks and fire interaction (mod_fs2r_11)
df_fs2r_predgrid <- df_fs2r %>%
  filter(total_stocks < 100) %>%
  group_by(fire) %>%
  summarise(
    min_ts = min(total_stocks, na.rm = TRUE),
    max_ts = max(total_stocks, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = 'drop') %>%
  rowwise() %>%
  mutate(total_stocks_seq = list(seq(min_ts, max_ts, length.out = 100))) %>%
  unnest(total_stocks_seq) %>%
  rename(total_stocks = total_stocks_seq)

# Predict
pred_link <- predict(mod_fs2r_11, newdata = df_fs2r_predgrid, type = 'link', se.fit = TRUE)

df_fs2r_predgrid <- df_fs2r_predgrid %>%
  mutate(
    fit   = exp(pred_link$fit),
    lower = exp(pred_link$fit - 1.96 * pred_link$se.fit),
    upper = exp(pred_link$fit + 1.96 * pred_link$se.fit),
    fire_label = ifelse(fire, 'Fire', 'No Fire'))

# Plot
ggplot(df_fs2r_predgrid, aes(x = total_stocks, y = fit, color = fire_label, fill = fire_label)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lower, ymax = upper), alpha = 0.15, color = NA) +
  geom_line(size = 1) +
  geom_jitter(
    data = df_fs2r %>% filter(total_stocks < 100 & fire_label == 'No Fire'),
    aes(x = total_stocks, y = recruit_count_t1, color = fire_label),
    alpha = 0.1, size = 1.8, width = 0.3, height = 0) +
  geom_jitter(
    data = df_fs2r %>% filter(total_stocks < 100 & fire_label == 'Fire'),
    aes(x = total_stocks, y = recruit_count_t1, color = fire_label),
    alpha = 0.5, size = 1.8, width = 0.3, height = 0) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c('No Fire' = '#1b9e77', 'Fire' = '#d95f02')) +
  scale_fill_manual( values = c('No Fire' = '#1b9e77', 'Fire' = '#d95f02')) +
  labs(
    x = 'Total Flowering Stems (t)',
    y = 'Predicted Recruitment Count (t+1)',
    title = 'Effect of Fire and Flowering Stems on Recruitment',
    color = 'Fire in Previous Year',
    fill  = 'Fire in Previous Year') +
  theme_bw(base_size = 14)

                nr_total_indiv = n(),
                fire = any(fire == T),
                .groups = 'drop'), 
            by = c('site', 'quad', 'year')) %>%
  full_join(df %>%
              group_by(site, quad, year) %>%
              summarise(
                recruit_count_t1 = sum(recruits, na.rm = TRUE),
                .groups = 'drop') %>%
              mutate(year = year - 1), 
            by = c('site', 'quad', 'year')) %>% 
  drop_na()

# Models
mod_2r_00 <- glm.nb(recruit_count_t1 ~ fire,                  data = df_2r)
mod_2r_11 <- glm.nb(recruit_count_t1 ~ total_stocks   + fire, data = df_2r)
mod_2r_12 <- glm.nb(recruit_count_t1 ~ total_stocks   * fire, data = df_2r)
mod_2r_21 <- glm.nb(recruit_count_t1 ~ nr_repro_indiv + fire, data = df_2r)
mod_2r_22 <- glm.nb(recruit_count_t1 ~ nr_repro_indiv * fire, data = df_2r)
mod_2r_31 <- glm.nb(recruit_count_t1 ~ nr_total_indiv + fire, data = df_2r)
mod_2r_32 <- glm.nb(recruit_count_t1 ~ nr_total_indiv * fire, data = df_2r)

mods_2r      <- list(
  mod_2r_00, mod_2r_11, mod_2r_12, mod_2r_21, mod_2r_22, mod_2r_31, mod_2r_32)
mods_2r_dAIC <- AICctab(mods_2r, weights = T, sort = F)$dAIC

4 Models

5 Updated data

This chapter documents the updated Polygala lewtonii dataset and the construction of the revised working data. The new dataset is not simply an extension of the data described in Chapter @ref(data). It adds observations from more recent years, reorganizes the original data structure, and provides additional information at the individual, quadrat, and site levels. Consequently, the complete data-processing workflow was reviewed and updated.

The main aim of this chapter is to describe the newly provided files, compare them with the data used in Chapter @ref(data), document the decisions made during data cleaning, and explain how the final working dataset was produced.

5.1 Overview

The updated data were provided as an Excel workbook containing four principal worksheets: Demog_longform, Demog, QuadLevel, and SiteHistory. Each worksheet is accompanied by separate metadata describing its variables and coding.

The demographic records now extend through 2025. In addition to the longer study period, the updated workbook separates repeated demographic observations, quadrat-level information, and site-level management history more clearly than the dataset used in Chapter @ref(data). These structural changes required us to reassess plant identity, annual transitions, recruitment, mortality, growth, and disturbance exposure before constructing the revised working dataset.

Code 
library(dplyr)

file_workbook <- paste0(
  "C:/code/RUPDemo_IPMs/archbold/data/pole/",
  "Pol_lew_CCS_2025_complete.xlsx")

df_workbook_sheets <- tibble(
  sheet = readxl::excel_sheets(file_workbook)) %>%
  mutate(
    type = if_else(
      str_detect(sheet, "metadata$"),
      "Metadata", "Data"),
    dataset = str_remove(sheet, " metadata$")) %>%
  dplyr::select(dataset, type, sheet)

knitr::kable(
  df_workbook_sheets,
  col.names = c("Dataset", "Worksheet type", "Worksheet name"))

5.2 Data worksheets

5.2.1 Demog_longform

Demog_longform is the main demographic dataset used in this analysis. It contains 43,869 observations and 12 variables. Each row represents one individual plant during one quarterly census. Plants are identified by a unique individual ID and linked to their quadrat and patch.

Survival was recorded during the quarterly censuses in March, June, September, and December. Stage, height, maximum crown diameter, stem number, and flowering stem number were generally recorded during the annual March census. The first annual census was carried out in April 2001.

Compared with the dataset used in Chapter @ref(data), the updated long-format dataset extends the demographic record through 2025 and already contains a consistent unique_ID.

Code

5.2.2 Demog

Demog contains 7,424 rows and 309 columns. It stores the demographic history in wide format, with one row per individual and separate columns for each census date. For example, survival, stage, height, crown diameter, stem number, and flowering stem number are stored in variables such as surv0325, stg0325, and ht0325.

The two demographic worksheets therefore contain much of the same underlying information but organize it differently. Demog retains additional information such as cohort, plant position, comments, annual-survival variables, and historical post-burn measurements.

5.2.3 QuadLevel

QuadLevel contains one row for each of the 220 permanent quadrats. It includes the quadrat coordinates, treatment block, patch, monitoring level, recent plant counts, flowering-stem counts, stem counts, occupancy, and measurements of the 2022 prescribed burn.

This worksheet is particularly important for understanding the change in sampling after June 2022. Some quadrats continued under Level 3 individual demographic monitoring, whereas the remaining quadrats were reduced to Level 2 count-based monitoring. The Level 2 observations are stored in this worksheet rather than in the individual demographic dataset.

  dplyr::slice_head(n = 10) %>%

5.2.4 SiteHistory

SiteHistory provides a chronological record of major natural disturbances and management events at the study site. The worksheet includes prescribed burns in 2001, 2007, 2009, 2015, 2019, 2020, and 2022, several hurricanes in 2004, Hurricane Irma in 2017, and hardwood reduction in 2023.

This is an important addition to the data described in Chapter @ref(data), which only included the four prescribed burns up to 2015. Fire is central to the demography of P. lewtonii: established plants are commonly killed by fire, while large seedling cohorts can recruit from the persistent soil seedbank after burning. Other disturbances, including hurricanes and hardwood removal, may also alter survival, recruitment, vegetation cover, and the availability of open habitat. Disturbance history is therefore treated as a central part of the demographic data rather than only as background site information.

Note to the data provider: The date recorded for the 2015 prescribed burn incorrectly gives the year 2025. This is a known typographical error, and the event is treated as a 2015 burn throughout the analysis.

5.3 Differences from the previous dataset

The updated dataset differs from the data used in Chapter @ref(data) in both its time span and structure. The earlier dataset covered the monitoring period from 2001 to 2017, whereas the updated demographic records extend through 2025.

Aspect Previous dataset Updated dataset
Study period 2001–2017 2001–2025
Plant identity Identity reconstructed from management unit, quadrat, plant tag, angle, and distance A unique individual identifier is supplied

The supplied unique individual identifier is an improvement. In the previous analysis, plant tags were not always unique through time and plant identity therefore had to be reconstructed from the tag and its position within the quadrat. The updated unique_ID variable removes this step and is used as the individual identifier throughout the revised data preparation.

The updated workbook also separates information that was previously combined within the demographic records. Repeated demographic observations are taken from Demog_longform, while additional individual, quadrat, and disturbance information can be obtained from the other worksheets. This provides more information, but also requires the different spatial and temporal levels of the data to be handled explicitly.

The revised working-data procedure was therefore rebuilt rather than simply applied to the additional years. In particular, recruitment timing, annual survival, growth transitions, and disturbance exposure were checked again against the quarterly census structure.

5.4 Construction of the annual demographic dataset

The demographic data contain quarterly observations, but the IPMs describe transitions between annual censuses. The annual dataset was therefore created by retaining records with a recorded stage. Stage, plant size, stem number, and flowering stem number were normally measured during the March census. The initial annual census was conducted in April 2001.

Annual census records were identified by the presence of a stage classification. Unlike filtering by height or crown diameter, this approach also retains individuals with incomplete size measurements, including confirmed recruits that could not be assigned a volume.

Code 
df_annual <- df_demog_long %>%
  rename(id = unique_id) %>%
  filter(!is.na(stg)) %>%
  arrange(id, year, month)

n_annual_duplicates <- df_annual %>%
  count(id, year) %>%
  filter(n > 1) %>%
  nrow()

df_annual_summary <- df_annual %>%
  summarise(
    records = n(),
    individuals = n_distinct(id),
    quadrats = n_distinct(quad),
    sites = n_distinct(patch),
    first_year = min(year, na.rm = TRUE),
    last_year = max(year, na.rm = TRUE))

knitr::kable(
  df_annual_summary,
  col.names = c(
    "Annual records", "Individuals", "Quadrats", "Sites",
    "First year", "Last year"))
Annual records Individuals Quadrats Sites First year Last year
10510 5856 170 25 2001 2025

Each row in the resulting dataset represents one individual at one annual census. No duplicated individual-year records were found (0 cases).

Code 
df_census_timing <- df_annual %>%
  group_by(month) %>%
  summarise(
    first_year = min(year, na.rm = TRUE),
    last_year = max(year, na.rm = TRUE),
    years = n_distinct(year),
    records = n(),
    .groups = "drop")

knitr::kable(
  df_census_timing,
  col.names = c(

    "Number of years", "Annual records"))
Census month First year Last year Number of years Annual records
3 2002 2025 24 10250
4 2001 2001 1 260

The April records belong exclusively to the first census in 2001. All subsequent annual records were collected in March. The annual transition represented by a row therefore generally begins in March of year \(t\) and ends in March of year \(t+1\). The first transition begins in April 2001 and ends in March 2002.

5.5 Recruitment

Recruitment was identified from the quarterly survival code qsurv == 5, which records the first observation of an individual as a seedling. Recruitment was assigned to the annual census at the end of the corresponding census interval.

Seedlings recorded during March were assigned to that census year. Seedlings first recorded from June to December were assigned to the following annual census. Recruitment in 2001 was left as unknown because the first census represents the beginning of the study rather than a complete annual recruitment interval.

Code 
df_recruit <- df_demog_long %>%
  filter(qsurv == 5) %>%
  transmute(
    id = unique_id,
    recruit_year = case_when(
      year == 2001 & month == 4 ~ 2001,
      month > 3 ~ year + 1,
      TRUE ~ year)) %>%
  distinct(id, recruit_year) %>%
  mutate(recruit_qsurv = 1)

df_annual_recruit <- df_annual %>%
  left_join(
    df_recruit,
    by = c("id", "year" = "recruit_year")) %>%
  mutate(
    recruit = case_when(
      year == 2001 ~ NA_real_,
      recruit_qsurv == 1 ~ 1,
      TRUE ~ 0))

df_recruit_summary <- df_annual_recruit %>%
  summarise(
    confirmed_recruits = sum(recruit == 1, na.rm = TRUE),
    non_recruits = sum(recruit == 0, na.rm = TRUE),
    baseline_unknown = sum(is.na(recruit)))

knitr::kable(
  df_recruit_summary,
  col.names = c(
    "Confirmed recruits", "Non-recruits",
    "Unknown baseline records"))
Confirmed recruits Non-recruits Unknown baseline records
5535 4715 260

The previous preparation combined three criteria: the immediately preceding quarterly survival code, the current quarterly survival code, and annual stage 1. This could miss seedlings first observed earlier in the annual interval if later quarterly observations occurred before the annual census.

The revised method searches the complete interval for a confirmed seedling record and does not depend on the immediately preceding observation. Annual stage is not used to define recruitment. Individuals recorded as new adults (qsurv == 3) are also not classified as recruits because their seedling status during that year cannot be confirmed. :contentReferenceoaicite:0

5.6 Survival and growth transitions

Survival and growth were defined over the interval between consecutive annual censuses. All recorded deaths (qsurv == 0) occurring after the census in year \(t\) and no later than the census in year \(t+1\) were assigned to that annual transition.

A recorded death was treated as direct evidence of mortality during the annual transition. In a small number of cases, an individual was coded as dead during one quarterly census but was recorded again at a later quarterly census within the same annual interval. However, the individual was absent from the next full annual census and did not appear in subsequent annual records. The later quarterly observation was therefore not interpreted as survival to \(t+1\).

The annual transition containing the death was classified as survives = 0. Any later quarterly size measurement within that interval was not used as the individual’s size at \(t+1\), so the transition was also excluded from the growth data.

Census Observation Interpretation
March, year \(t\) Individual measured during the annual census Alive at \(t\)
June, year \(t\) Individual coded as dead (qsurv = 0) Death occurred during the transition
September, year \(t\) Individual recorded again during a quarterly census Does not override the death record
March, year \(t+1\) Individual absent from the annual census survives = 0; no growth transition
Code 
df_death_interval <- df_demog_long %>%
  filter(!is.na(stg)) %>%
  transmute(
    id = unique_id, year,
    census_time = year * 12 + month,
    target_time = (year + 1) * 12 + 3) %>%
  left_join(
    df_demog_long %>%
      filter(qsurv == 0) %>%
      transmute(
        id = unique_id,
        death_time = year * 12 + month),
    by = "id", relationship = "many-to-many") %>%
  group_by(id, year) %>%
  summarise(
    death_in_interval = any(
      !is.na(death_time) &
        death_time > census_time &
        death_time <= target_time),
    .groups = "drop")

df_transitions <- df_annual_recruit %>%
  left_join(df_death_interval, by = c("id", "year")) %>%
  mutate(
    death_in_interval = replace_na(death_in_interval, FALSE)) %>%
  group_by(id) %>%
  arrange(year, month, .by_group = TRUE) %>%
  mutate(
    next_year = lead(year),
    last_observed_year = max(year, na.rm = TRUE),
    annual_transition = coalesce(next_year == year + 1, FALSE),
    observed_later = last_observed_year > year,
    valid_growth_transition =
      annual_transition & !death_in_interval,
    survives = case_when(
      death_in_interval ~ 0,
      annual_transition ~ 1,
      observed_later ~ 1,
      TRUE ~ NA_real_)) %>%
  ungroup()

df_transition_summary <- df_transitions %>%
  summarise(
    recorded_deaths = sum(death_in_interval),
    observed_survival = sum(
      annual_transition & !death_in_interval),
    inferred_survival = sum(
      observed_later & !annual_transition &
        !death_in_interval),
    unknown_survival = sum(is.na(survives)),
    growth_transitions = sum(valid_growth_transition))

knitr::kable(
  df_transition_summary,
  col.names = c(
    "Recorded deaths",
    "Observed survival",
    "Survival inferred from later observations",
    "Unknown survival",
    "Valid growth transitions"))
Recorded deaths Observed survival Survival inferred from later observations Unknown survival Valid growth transitions
5056 4321 301 832 4321

When an individual was not recorded in year \(t+1\), but was observed again in a later year, it was considered to have survived the first transition. This accounts for known gaps in annual sampling. Growth was not reconstructed across these gaps because no consecutive size measurement was available.

Growth measurements at \(t+1\) were retained only when the individual was recorded in the following annual census and no death occurred during the transition.

5.7 Disturbance

Disturbance was assigned at the quadrat level rather than the site level. Prescribed burns did not affect every quadrat within a site equally. In the updated data, several site-year combinations contain both disturbed and undisturbed quadrats. Aggregating disturbance to the site level would therefore remove observed spatial variation.

The disturbance variable describes whether a quadrat was affected by fire during an annual transition. A recorded fire effect was coded as 1 and an explicitly unburned quadrat was coded as 0. A missing classification was retained as NA, because it provides no evidence that the quadrat was unburned.

5.7.1 Source of the 2022 fire classification

Fire information through 2020 was obtained from the historical post-burn variables in Demog. The 2022 fire classification was instead obtained from QuadLevel.

The metadata for postburn_status0322 distinguishes three possible values: 1 for burned, 0 for unburned, and NA for a missing plot. However, the workbook does not establish why a classification is missing. A missing value could represent a missing field observation, incomplete data entry, or another unrecorded reason. It is therefore described here simply as having no recorded classification.

The two worksheets were compared before selecting the source of the 2022 variable.

Code 
df_dist_2022_demog <- df_demog_wide %>%
  filter(!is.na(quad)) %>%
  group_by(quad) %>%
  summarise(
    dist_2022_demog = if_else(
      all(is.na(postburn_status0322)),
      NA_real_,
      as.numeric(
        any(postburn_status0322 == 1, na.rm = TRUE))),
    .groups = "drop")

df_dist_2022 <- df_quad %>%
  transmute(
    quad,
    dist_2022 = as.numeric(postburn_status0322))

df_2022_source_summary <- df_dist_2022 %>%
  left_join(
    df_dist_2022_demog,
    by = "quad") %>%
  summarise(
    quadrats = n(),
    missing_in_quadlevel = sum(is.na(dist_2022)),
    missing_in_demog = sum(is.na(dist_2022_demog)),
    available_in_quadlevel_but_missing_in_demog = sum(
      !is.na(dist_2022) &
        is.na(dist_2022_demog)),
    conflicting_values = sum(
      !is.na(dist_2022) &
        !is.na(dist_2022_demog) &
        dist_2022 != dist_2022_demog))

knitr::kable(
  df_2022_source_summary,
  col.names = c(
    "Quadrats",
    "Missing in QuadLevel",
    "Missing in Demog",
    "Available only in QuadLevel",
    "Conflicting values"))
Quadrats Missing in QuadLevel Missing in Demog Available only in QuadLevel Conflicting values
220 1 126 125 0

QuadLevel contained an explicit 2022 classification for 125 quadrats that lacked the corresponding information in Demog. There were 0 conflicts among quadrats with information in both worksheets. QuadLevel was therefore used as the source of the 2022 fire classification.

Only 1 actual quadrat lacked a recorded 2022 classification. This quadrat was retained as NA rather than being added to the explicitly unburned group.

5.7.2 Assignment to annual transitions

For the fires through 2020, a positive post-burn category was coded as 1 and a recorded category of zero was coded as 0. If all relevant measurements were missing during a known fire event, the classification remained NA. The 2022 classification was joined from QuadLevel.

Code 
df_dist_event <- df_demog_wide %>%
  filter(!is.na(quad)) %>%
  group_by(quad) %>%
  summarise(
    dist_2001 = if_else(
      all(is.na(postburn_status1201)), NA_real_,
      as.numeric(any(
        postburn_status1201 > 0,
        na.rm = TRUE))),
    dist_2007 = if_else(
      all(is.na(postburn_pct1207)), NA_real_,
      as.numeric(any(
        postburn_pct1207 > 0,
        na.rm = TRUE))),
    dist_2009 = if_else(
      all(is.na(postburn_pct0609)), NA_real_,
      as.numeric(any(
        postburn_pct0609 > 0,
        na.rm = TRUE))),
    dist_2015 = if_else(
      all(is.na(postburn_pct0615)), NA_real_,
      as.numeric(any(
        postburn_pct0615 > 0,

      as.numeric(any(

      all(is.na(postburn_pct0120)), NA_real_,
      as.numeric(any(
        postburn_pct0120 > 0,

  left_join(
    df_dist_2022,

df_dist_transition <- bind_rows(
  df_dist_event %>%

df_transitions_dist <- df_transitions %>%

2020 Demog postburn_pct0120 2019 2
2022 QuadLevel postburn_status0322 2021 0

The fire event was assigned to the annual transition during which it occurred. The fires in 2001, 2007, 2009, and 2015 occurred after the annual census and were assigned to transitions beginning in those years. The fires in 2019, 2020, and 2022 were assigned to the transitions ending in those years.

Disturbance differed among quadrats within 29 site-year combinations, supporting its retention at the quadrat level. In total, 2 annual records have no recorded fire classification during a known fire transition. The number associated with each fire is reported in the final column of the table.

5.8 Final working dataset

The cleaned annual records were exported as the working dataset used by the demographic models. The dataset retains the site, quadrat, individual, and year identifiers so that observations can be analysed at the appropriate spatial and temporal levels.

Code 
file_workdata <- file.path(
  dirname(file_workbook),
  "ab_pole_df_workdata_260519.csv")

df_work <- readr::read_csv(
  file_workdata,
  show_col_types = FALSE)

df_work_summary <- df_work %>%
  summarise(
    records = n(),
    individuals = n_distinct(id),
    quadrats = n_distinct(quad),
    sites = n_distinct(site),
    first_year = min(year, na.rm = TRUE),
    last_year = max(year, na.rm = TRUE),
    recruits = sum(recruit == 1, na.rm = TRUE),
    deaths = sum(survives == 0, na.rm = TRUE))

knitr::kable(

Records Individuals Quadrats Sites First year Last year Recruits Deaths
10510 5856 170 25 2001 2025 5535 5056

Each row represents one individual at one annual census. Variables measured at the beginning of the transition are labelled with t0, while measurements from the following annual census are labelled with t1. A t1 measurement is only available when the individual has a valid transition to the next annual census.

The final dataset includes height, crown diameter, stem number, flowering stem number, stage, recruitment, survival, growth, and quadrat-level disturbance. Plant volume was calculated as a cylindrical size index:

\[ \text{volume} = \pi \left(\frac{\text{crown diameter}}{2}\right)^2 \times \text{height}. \]

Log-transformed height and volume variables, including quadratic and cubic terms, were added for later comparison of nonlinear vital-rate models.

Missing size_t1 and volume_t1 values mainly represent individuals without a valid consecutive annual transition. Missing volume_t0 values occur mainly among recruits for which crown diameter was not measured. These recruits are retained in the dataset because they still contribute to recruitment counts, even when they cannot be used in volume-based vital-rate models.

Disturbance remains missing when no fire classification is recorded for a quadrat during a known fire event. The available data do not establish why a classification is missing. These observations were therefore retained as unknown rather than being classified as undisturbed.

fig_sampling

Because this figure is constructed from individual records in Demog_longform, the absence of a point means that no individual demographic record is available for that quadrat-year. It does not necessarily demonstrate that the quadrat was not visited. This distinction is especially important after 2022, when Level 2 quadrats continued to provide quadrat-level counts but no longer contributed complete individual demographic records.

5.10 Monitoring levels after 2022

Following the 2022 field season, monitoring was reduced in a subset of the permanent quadrats. The variable lvl3 identifies whether a quadrat continued under Level 3 individual demographic monitoring or was monitored using the reduced Level 2 protocol.

The two monitoring levels contain different types of information:

knitr::kable(df_level_definition)
Feature Level 2 Level 3
Observation unit Whole quadrat Individually marked plants
Information recorded Total plants, flowering stems and stems within the quadrat Survival, recruitment, stage, size and flowering of individual plants
Main worksheet QuadLevel Demog_longform
Use in this project Population counts and monitoring effort Annual transitions and vital-rate models

Level 3 monitoring follows individual plants through time. It therefore provides the information required to estimate individual survival, growth, flowering and recruitment. These records are stored in Demog_longform and form the basis of the annual working dataset.

Level 2 monitoring does not follow individual plants. Instead, the field team records quadrat-level totals, including the number of plants, flowering stems and stems. These observations are stored in QuadLevel. Level 2 quadrats therefore remain part of the monitoring programme, but they cannot provide individual annual transitions.

The distribution of quadrats between the two monitoring levels and the availability of recent count data are shown below.

This distinction is important when interpreting changes in the number of records after 2022. A reduction in individual records does not necessarily represent a decline in the population. It can also reflect the change from Level 3 individual monitoring to Level 2 quadrat-level counts.

The working dataset is constructed from Demog_longform and therefore uses individual-level observations. Level 2 data must be analysed separately or explicitly incorporated as quadrat-level counts. Raw population totals from the working dataset should consequently not be compared across the monitoring change without accounting for the number and type of quadrats sampled.

6 Mean IPM with fire for Polygala lewtonii

6.1 What this mean IPM does

This chapter develops a deterministic mean integral projection model (IPM) for Polygala lewtonii using demographic records from 2001 through 2025. The model pools observations across years and sites to estimate average vital-rate relationships, while retaining fire as an explicit quadrat-level predictor. It is therefore a mean model: it describes expected demographic performance under specified fire conditions rather than reconstructing the demographic conditions of each individual year or site.

The continuous state variable is log plant volume. For a plant of size \(z\) in year \(t\), the IPM projects the density of plant sizes in year \(t+1\) using a survival-growth component and a fertility component,

\[ K(z',z) = P(z',z) + F(z',z). \]

Current-year fire affects survival, growth, and the quadrat-level conversion of flowering stems to recruits. Fire in the previous year affects flowering probability and flowering-stem production. The model therefore distinguishes four fire states:

  1. no fire in either year;
  2. current-year fire only;
  3. previous-year fire only; and
  4. fire in both years.

A fifth kernel averages these four state-specific kernels using their observed frequencies among quadrat-years. The model reports both the dominant eigenvalue of each kernel, which is the asymptotic population growth rate, and the one-step growth rate obtained by projecting the mean observed size distribution.

6.2 Main assumptions and interpretation

The model makes the following assumptions.

  1. Mean demographic relationships. Survival, growth, flowering, and recruitment relationships are pooled across years and sites. No year or site random effects are included. Year and site are retained only for data construction, disturbance timing, recruitment transitions, and validation.

  2. Annual and time-homogeneous transitions. Each kernel represents an annual transition under one fixed combination of current and previous-year fire. Within a fire state, the fitted vital-rate relationships are assumed not to change through time.

  3. Quadrat-level fire. Fire exposure is assigned at the quadrat-year level. Current fire and previous-year fire remain separate because they affect different demographic processes.

  4. Size is the continuous plant state. Individual heterogeneity other than size and fire exposure is not modeled explicitly.

  5. Phenomenological recruitment model. Total flowering stems in quadrat \(q\) during year \(t\) predict recruits in the same quadrat during year \(t+1\). Recruitment may occur when no flowering stems are recorded because the intercept represents emergence from the persistent seedbank. The negative flowering-stem coefficient, especially after fire, is interpreted as a possible density or establishment effect rather than as direct evidence of parent-specific fecundity.

  6. No explicit seedbank stage. The persistent seedbank is represented indirectly by the recruitment intercept and fire response. Predicted quadrat recruitment is converted to recruits per flowering stem at a quadrat-level reference stem abundance and allocated among plants according to expected flowering-stem production. This keeps the kernel linear but does not imply known parentage.

  7. Deterministic projection. The kernels do not include environmental stochasticity, demographic stochasticity, or parameter uncertainty.

  8. Observed fire-state mixture. The expected-regime kernel uses observed quadrat-year frequencies as fixed weights. The fire-in-both-years state is retained, but it is supported by only one observed quadrat-year and must be interpreted cautiously.

  9. Mean initial size distribution. The one-step projected growth rate uses the arithmetic mean of annual observed size-frequency vectors. Recruits without a usable size measurement are distributed across the fitted recruit size distribution.

  10. Observed-growth validation is incomplete. Annual abundance change is calculated only from quadrats containing individual records in both consecutive years. Historically sampled but empty quadrats cannot be reconstructed consistently, so this comparison describes matched occupied quadrats rather than a complete census of all sampled quadrats.

The chapter contains the full analysis code. It does not source the completed IPM script as a shortcut.

6.3 Set up the analysis

Code 
set.seed(100)
options(stringsAsFactors = FALSE)

6.3.1 Model specification

Code 
v_head <- 'archbold'
v_species <- 'Polygala lewtonii'
v_years_re <- c()

v_sp_abb <- tolower(
  gsub(
    ' ', '',
    paste(
      substr(unlist(strsplit(v_species, ' ')), 1, 2),
      collapse = '')))

v_script_prefix <- v_head
v_ggp_suffix <- paste(tools::toTitleCase(v_head), '-', v_species)

# Empty vectors select the best-supported polynomial by AICc.
v_mod_set_su <- c()
v_mod_set_gr <- c()
v_mod_set_fl <- c()
v_mod_set_fl_n <- c()
v_mod_set_re <- c()

6.4.1 Load the completed workdata

The workdata already contains current-year disturbance and disturbance in the exact previous year. These fields are retained directly rather than rebuilt from the subset of observed individual rows.

Code 
df <- read.csv(
  file.path(
    dir_data,
    paste0('ab_', v_sp_abb, '_df_workdata_260519.csv'))) %>%
  mutate(
    disturbance = as.numeric(dist_transition),
    disturbance_prev = as.numeric(disturbance_prev),
    year = as.integer(year),
    site = factor(site)) %>%
  filter(
    !is.na(year),
    !(year %in% v_years_re))

6.5 Construct the vital-rate data sets

6.5.1 Survival

Code 
df_su <- df %>%
  filter(
    !is.na(survives),
    size_t0 != 0,
    is.finite(logvol_t0),
    is.finite(logvol_t0_2),
    is.finite(logvol_t0_3),
    !is.na(disturbance)) %>%
  dplyr::select(
    id, site, year, size_t0, survives, size_t1,
    logsize_t0, logsize_t1, logsize_t0_2, logsize_t0_3,
    volume_t0, volume_t1, logvol_t0, logvol_t1,
    logvol_t0_2, logvol_t0_3, disturbance, stage)

6.5.2 Growth

Code 
df_gr <- df %>%
  filter(
    size_t0 != 0,
    size_t1 != 0,
    is.finite(logvol_t0),
    is.finite(logvol_t1),
    is.finite(logvol_t0_2),
    is.finite(logvol_t0_3),
    !is.na(disturbance)) %>%
  dplyr::select(
    id, site, year, size_t0, size_t1,
    logsize_t0, logsize_t1, logsize_t0_2, logsize_t0_3,
    volume_t0, volume_t1, logvol_t0, logvol_t1,
    logvol_t0_2, logvol_t0_3, disturbance, stage)

6.5.3 Flowering probability and flowering-stem number

Observed recruits are retained because some recruits flowered.

Code 
df_fl <- df %>%
  filter(
    !is.na(flower),
    is.finite(logvol_t0),
    is.finite(logvol_t0_2),
    is.finite(logvol_t0_3),
    !is.na(disturbance_prev)) %>%
  dplyr::select(
    id, site, year, size_t0, flower, fl_nr, size_t1,
    logsize_t0, logsize_t1, logsize_t0_2, logsize_t0_3,
    volume_t0, volume_t1, logvol_t0, logvol_t1,
    logvol_t0_2, logvol_t0_3, disturbance_prev, stage, recruits)

df_fl_cond <- df_fl %>%
  filter(
    flower == 1,
    !is.na(fl_nr),
    fl_nr > 0,
    fl_nr == round(fl_nr))

6.5.4 Quadrat-level flowering stems and recruits

Total flowering stems in quadrat \(q\) during year \(t\) predict recruits in the same quadrat during year \(t+1\). A quadrat transition is retained only when the same quadrat has individual records in both years.

Code 
df_quad_year_sampled <- df %>%
  distinct(site, quad, year)

df_fs2r <- df %>%
  group_by(site, quad, year) %>%
  summarise(
    fs_t0 = sum(fl_nr, na.rm = TRUE),
    disturbance = if_else(
      all(is.na(disturbance)),
      NA_real_,
      max(disturbance, na.rm = TRUE)),
    .groups = 'drop') %>%
  mutate(
    year_t1 = year + 1) %>%
  semi_join(
    df_quad_year_sampled %>%
      transmute(
        site,
        quad,
        year_t1 = year),
    by = c(
      'site',
      'quad',
      'year_t1')) %>%
  left_join(
    df %>%
      filter(recruits == 1) %>%
      count(
        site,
        quad,
        year,
        name = 're_t1'),
    by = c(
      'site',
      'quad',
      'year_t1' = 'year')) %>%
  mutate(
    re_t1 = replace_na(re_t1, 0L),
    site = factor(site),
    fs_t0_log = log1p(fs_t0),
    re_t1_log = log1p(re_t1)) %>%
  filter(
    !is.na(year),
    !is.na(year_t1),
    !is.na(disturbance),
    !(year %in% v_years_re),
    !(year_t1 %in% v_years_re))

df_fs2r %>%
  summarise(
    quadrats = n_distinct(quad),
    transitions = n(),
    zero_stems = sum(fs_t0 == 0),
    zero_recruits = sum(re_t1 == 0),
    burned_transitions = sum(disturbance == 1),
    unburned_transitions = sum(disturbance == 0))

6.6 Fit the mean vital-rate models

Candidate models use intercept-only, fire-only, and first- through third-order size polynomials, each with and without the relevant fire term. Empty model-set vectors select the model with the lowest AICc.

6.6.1 Survival model

Code 
mod_su_00 <- glm(
  survives ~ 1,
  data = df_su,
  family = binomial)

mod_su_0 <- glm(
  survives ~ disturbance,
  data = df_su,
  family = binomial)

mod_su_10 <- glm(
  survives ~ logvol_t0,
  data = df_su,
  family = binomial)

mod_su_1 <- glm(
  survives ~ logvol_t0 + disturbance,
  data = df_su,
  family = binomial)

mod_su_20 <- glm(
  survives ~ logvol_t0 + logvol_t0_2,
  data = df_su,
  family = binomial)

mod_su_2 <- glm(
  survives ~ logvol_t0 + logvol_t0_2 + disturbance,
  data = df_su,
  family = binomial)

mod_su_30 <- glm(
  survives ~ logvol_t0 + logvol_t0_2 + logvol_t0_3,
  data = df_su,
  family = binomial)

mod_su_3 <- glm(
  survives ~ logvol_t0 + logvol_t0_2 + logvol_t0_3 +
    disturbance,
  data = df_su,
  family = binomial)

mods_su <- list(
  mod_su_00, mod_su_0, mod_su_10, mod_su_1,
  mod_su_20, mod_su_2, mod_su_30, mod_su_3)

mods_su_dAICc <- bbmle::AICctab(
  mods_su,
  weights = TRUE,
  sort = FALSE)$dAICc

mods_su_sorted <- order(mods_su_dAICc)

if (length(v_mod_set_su) == 0) {
  mod_su_index_best <- mods_su_sorted[1]
} else {
  mod_su_index_best <- v_mod_set_su + 1
}

v_mod_su_index <- floor((mod_su_index_best - 1) / 2)
mod_su_best <- mods_su[[mod_su_index_best]]

summary(mod_su_best)

6.6.3 Growth variance

Growth variance is modeled as an exponential function of the fitted growth mean.

Code 
mod_gr_x <- fitted(mod_gr_best)
mod_gr_y <- resid(mod_gr_best)^2

mod_gr_var <- nls(
  mod_gr_y ~ a * exp(b * mod_gr_x),
  start = list(a = 1, b = 0),
  control = nls.control(
    maxiter = 1000,
    tol = 1e-6,
    warnOnly = TRUE))

summary(mod_gr_var)

6.6.6 Flowering-stem-to-recruit model

The recruitment candidates allow a seedbank intercept, a current-fire effect, a flowering-stem effect, and their interaction. No year or site random effects are fitted.

Code 
mod_re_00 <- lm(
  re_t1_log ~ 1,
  data = df_fs2r)

mod_re_0 <- lm(
  re_t1_log ~ disturbance,
  data = df_fs2r)

mod_re_10 <- lm(
  re_t1_log ~ fs_t0_log,
  data = df_fs2r)

mod_re_1 <- lm(
  re_t1_log ~ fs_t0_log + disturbance,
  data = df_fs2r)

mod_re_20 <- lm(
  re_t1_log ~ fs_t0_log * disturbance,
  data = df_fs2r)

mods_re <- list(
  mod_re_00,
  mod_re_0,
  mod_re_10,
  mod_re_1,
  mod_re_20)

mods_re_dAICc <- bbmle::AICctab(
  mods_re,
  weights = TRUE,
  sort = FALSE)$dAICc

mods_re_sorted <- order(mods_re_dAICc)

if (length(v_mod_set_re) == 0) {
  mod_re_index_best <- mods_re_sorted[1]
} else {
  mod_re_index_best <- v_mod_set_re + 1
}

v_mod_re_index <- mod_re_index_best - 1
mod_re_best <- mods_re[[mod_re_index_best]]

6.6.7 Recruitment-model support

Code 
df_recruit_model_support <- tibble(
  model = c(
    'Intercept only',
    'Disturbance only',
    'Flowering stems',
    'Flowering stems + disturbance',
    'Full interaction'),
  dAICc = as.numeric(mods_re_dAICc)) %>%
  mutate(
    weight = exp(-0.5 * dAICc) /
      sum(exp(-0.5 * dAICc))) %>%
  arrange(dAICc)

knitr::kable(
  df_recruit_model_support,
  digits = c(NA, 2, 3),
  caption = paste(
    'AICc support for quadrat-level flowering-stem-to-recruit',
    'models.'))
(#tab:mean-ipm-recruitment-support)AICc support for quadrat-level flowering-stem-to-recruit models.
model dAICc weight
Full interaction 0.00 0.569
Disturbance only 1.56 0.260
Flowering stems + disturbance 2.40 0.171
Intercept only 52.77 0.000
Flowering stems 53.63 0.000

The full interaction model is selected. Its fitted form is

\[ \log(1 + R_{q,t+1}) = \beta_0 + \beta_1\log(1 + M_{q,t}) + \beta_d d_{q,t} + \beta_{1d}\log(1 + M_{q,t})d_{q,t} + \varepsilon, \]

where \(M_{q,t}\) is total flowering stems, \(R_{q,t+1}\) is the number of recruits in the same quadrat in the following year, and \(d_{q,t}\) indicates current fire.

6.6.8 Recruitment slopes and uncertainty

Code 
re_coef <- coef(mod_re_20)
re_vcov <- vcov(mod_re_20)

slope_unburned <- re_coef['fs_t0_log']

se_unburned <- sqrt(
  re_vcov[
    'fs_t0_log',
    'fs_t0_log'])

slope_burned <-
  re_coef['fs_t0_log'] +
  re_coef['fs_t0_log:disturbance']

se_burned <- sqrt(
  re_vcov[
    'fs_t0_log',
    'fs_t0_log'] +
  re_vcov[
    'fs_t0_log:disturbance',
    'fs_t0_log:disturbance'] +
  2 * re_vcov[
    'fs_t0_log',
    'fs_t0_log:disturbance'])

df_recruit_slopes <- tibble(
  disturbance = c(0, 1),
  slope = c(
    slope_unburned,
    slope_burned),
  lower_95 = c(
    slope_unburned - 1.96 * se_unburned,
    slope_burned - 1.96 * se_burned),
  upper_95 = c(
    slope_unburned + 1.96 * se_unburned,
    slope_burned + 1.96 * se_burned))

knitr::kable(
  df_recruit_slopes,
  digits = 3,

6.7 Plot the selected vital-rate models

Code 
make_mean_prediction <- function(data, model, disturbance_var) {
  x <- seq(
    min(data$logvol_t0, na.rm = TRUE),
    max(data$logvol_t0, na.rm = TRUE),
    length.out = 200)

  pred <- expand_grid(
    logvol_t0 = x,
    disturbance_value = c(0, 1)) %>%
    mutate(
      logvol_t0_2 = logvol_t0^2,
      logvol_t0_3 = logvol_t0^3,
      disturbance_plot = factor(
        disturbance_value,
        levels = c(0, 1),
        labels = c('No fire', 'Fire')))

  pred[[disturbance_var]] <- pred$disturbance_value
  pred$prediction <- predict(
    model,
    newdata = pred,
    type = 'response')

  pred
}

make_mean_plot <- function(
    data, model, response, disturbance_var, title, y_lab,
    probability = FALSE) {
  pred <- make_mean_prediction(
    data = data,
    model = model,
    disturbance_var = disturbance_var)

  data_plot <- data %>%
    mutate(
      disturbance_plot = factor(
        .data[[disturbance_var]],
        levels = c(0, 1),
        labels = c('No fire', 'Fire')))

  point_layer <- if (probability) {
    geom_jitter(
      data = data_plot,
      aes(
        x = logvol_t0,
        y = .data[[response]],
        color = disturbance_plot),
      alpha = 0.15,
      size = 0.7,
      width = 0.05,
      height = 0.05)
  } else {
    geom_point(
      data = data_plot,
      aes(
        x = logvol_t0,
        y = .data[[response]],
        color = disturbance_plot),
      alpha = 0.15,
      size = 0.7)
  }

  p <- ggplot() +
    point_layer +
    geom_line(
      data = pred,
      aes(
        x = logvol_t0,
        y = prediction,
        color = disturbance_plot),
      linewidth = 0.8) +
    scale_color_manual(
      values = c(
        'No fire' = 'black',
        'Fire' = 'red')) +
    theme_bw() +
    labs(
      title = title,
      subtitle = v_ggp_suffix,
      x = expression('log(volume)'[t0]),
      y = y_lab,
      color = NULL)

  if (probability) {
    p <- p + coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, 1))
  }

  p
}

6.9 Extract the selected model parameters

The extraction functions return zero for terms that are absent from the selected model. The same IPM functions can therefore use any selected candidate without manual coefficient changes.

Code 
size_term_map <- c(
  b0 = '(Intercept)',
  b1 = 'logvol_t0',
  b2 = 'logvol_t0_2',
  b3 = 'logvol_t0_3',
  bd = 'disturbance')

lagged_size_term_map <- c(
  b0 = '(Intercept)',
  b1 = 'logvol_t0',
  b2 = 'logvol_t0_2',
  b3 = 'logvol_t0_3',
  bd = 'disturbance_prev')

extract_terms <- function(model, prefix, term_map) {
  coefs <- stats::coef(model)

  values <- vapply(term_map, function(term_i) {
    if (term_i %in% names(coefs)) {
      unname(coefs[[term_i]])
    } else {
      0
    }
  }, numeric(1))

  names(values) <- paste0(prefix, names(term_map))
  values
}

extract_coef <- function(model, term, default = 0) {
  coefs <- stats::coef(model)

  if (term %in% names(coefs)) {
    unname(coefs[[term]])
  } else {
    default
  }
}

grow_var_coef <- stats::coef(mod_gr_var)

mesh_limits <- range(
  c(
    df_gr$logvol_t0,
    df_gr$logvol_t1,
    df_recr$logvol_t0),
  na.rm = TRUE,
  finite = TRUE)

mesh_limits <- c(
  mesh_limits[1] - 0.1,
  mesh_limits[2] + 0.1)

pars_mean <- as.list(c(
  extract_terms(
    mod_su_best,
    'surv_',
    size_term_map),
  extract_terms(
    mod_gr_best,
    'grow_',
    size_term_map),
  extract_terms(
    mod_fl_best,
    'fl_',
    lagged_size_term_map),
  extract_terms(
    mod_fl_n_best,
    'fln_',
    lagged_size_term_map),
  re_b0 = extract_coef(
    mod_re_best,
    '(Intercept)'),
  re_b1 = extract_coef(
    mod_re_best,
    'fs_t0_log'),
  re_bd = extract_coef(
    mod_re_best,
    'disturbance'),
  re_bf = extract_coef(
    mod_re_best,
    'fs_t0_log:disturbance'),
  re_sigma = stats::sigma(mod_re_best),
  recr_mean = rc_sz$mean,
  recr_sd = rc_sz$sd,
  grow_var_a = unname(grow_var_coef[['a']]),
  grow_var_b = unname(grow_var_coef[['b']]),
  fs_ref = mean(df_fs2r$fs_t0, na.rm = TRUE),
  L = mesh_limits[1],
  U = mesh_limits[2],
  mat_siz = 200,
  mod_su_index = v_mod_su_index,
  mod_gr_index = v_mod_gr_index,
  mod_fl_index = v_mod_fl_index,
  mod_fl_n_index = v_mod_fl_n_index,
  mod_re_index = v_mod_re_index))

pars_mean_table <- tibble(
  parameter = names(pars_mean),
  value = as.numeric(unlist(pars_mean)))

knitr::kable(
  pars_mean_table,

6.10 Define the IPM functions

6.10.1 General parameter and linear-predictor functions

Code 
get_par <- function(pars, par_name, default = 0) {
  if (!is.null(pars[[par_name]])) {
    pars[[par_name]]
  } else {
    default
  }
}

vital_lp <- function(x, pars, prefix, disturbance = 0) {
  get_par(pars, paste0(prefix, 'b0')) +
    get_par(pars, paste0(prefix, 'b1')) * x +
    get_par(pars, paste0(prefix, 'b2')) * x^2 +
    get_par(pars, paste0(prefix, 'b3')) * x^3 +
    get_par(pars, paste0(prefix, 'bd')) * disturbance
}

6.10.2 Survival

Code 
sx <- function(x, pars, disturbance = 0) {
  plogis(vital_lp(
    x = x,
    pars = pars,
    prefix = 'surv_',
    disturbance = disturbance))
}

6.10.3 Growth

Code 
grow_mu <- function(x, pars, disturbance = 0) {
  vital_lp(
    x = x,
    pars = pars,
    prefix = 'grow_',
    disturbance = disturbance)
}

grow_sd <- function(mean_value, pars) {
  variance <- get_par(pars, 'grow_var_a') *
    exp(get_par(pars, 'grow_var_b') * mean_value)

  sqrt(pmax(variance, .Machine$double.eps))
}

gxy <- function(x, y, pars, disturbance = 0) {
  mean_value <- grow_mu(
    x = x,
    pars = pars,
    disturbance = disturbance)

  sd_value <- grow_sd(
    mean_value = mean_value,
    pars = pars)

  dnorm(
    y,
    mean = mean_value,
    sd = sd_value)
}

6.10.4 Flowering probability and conditional flowering-stem number

Code 
fl_x <- function(x, pars, disturbance_prev = 0) {
  plogis(vital_lp(
    x = x,
    pars = pars,
    prefix = 'fl_',
    disturbance = disturbance_prev))
}

fln_x <- function(x, pars, disturbance_prev = 0) {
  exp(vital_lp(
    x = x,
    pars = pars,
    prefix = 'fln_',
    disturbance = disturbance_prev))
}

fs_x <- function(x, pars, disturbance_prev = 0) {
  fl_x(
    x = x,
    pars = pars,
    disturbance_prev = disturbance_prev) *
    fln_x(
      x = x,
      pars = pars,
      disturbance_prev = disturbance_prev)
}

6.10.5 Flowering-stem-to-recruit conversion

The coefficient extraction supports intercept-only, disturbance-only, flowering-stem, additive, and interaction models. Recruitment is not forced to zero when flowering stems equal zero because the fitted intercept represents seedbank emergence.

Code 
predict_recruits_from_stems <- function(
    flowering_stems, pars, disturbance = 0) {
  stems_nonnegative <- pmax(flowering_stems, 0)

  slope <- get_par(pars, 're_b1') +
    get_par(pars, 're_bf') * disturbance

  eta <- get_par(pars, 're_b0') +
    get_par(pars, 're_bd') * disturbance +
    slope * log1p(stems_nonnegative)

  recruits <- expm1(
    eta + 0.5 * get_par(pars, 're_sigma')^2)

  pmax(recruits, 0)
}

recruits_per_stem <- function(pars, disturbance = 0) {
  fs_ref <- get_par(pars, 'fs_ref', 0)

  if (!is.finite(fs_ref) || fs_ref <= 0) {
    return(0)
  }

  predict_recruits_from_stems(
    flowering_stems = fs_ref,
    pars = pars,
    disturbance = disturbance) / fs_ref
}

rx <- function(
    x, pars, disturbance = 0, disturbance_prev = 0) {
  fs_x(
    x = x,
    pars = pars,
    disturbance_prev = disturbance_prev) *
    recruits_per_stem(
      pars = pars,
      disturbance = disturbance)
}

The fitted model predicts nonzero recruitment from the seedbank when no current flowering stems are recorded.

Code 
tibble(
  disturbance = c(0, 1),
  predicted_recruits_zero_stems =
    predict_recruits_from_stems(
      flowering_stems = 0,
      pars = pars_mean,
      disturbance = disturbance))
