6.10.6 Recruit size distribution and fertility matrix

Code 
recr_y <- function(y, pars) {
  dnorm(
    y,
    mean = get_par(pars, 'recr_mean'),
    sd = get_par(pars, 'recr_sd'))
}

fy <- function(
    y, x, pars, h, disturbance = 0, disturbance_prev = 0) {
  Pvec <- recr_y(y, pars)
  recruit_mass <- sum(Pvec * h)

  if (!is.finite(recruit_mass) || recruit_mass <= 0) {
    stop('Recruit size distribution has no mass inside the mesh')
  }

  Pvec <- Pvec / recruit_mass

  Rvec <- rx(
    x = x,
    pars = pars,
    disturbance = disturbance,
    disturbance_prev = disturbance_prev)

  outer(Pvec, Rvec) * h
}

6.10.7 Full kernel

Code 
kernel <- function(
    pars, disturbance = 0, disturbance_prev = 0) {
  n <- as.integer(pars$mat_siz)
  L <- pars$L
  U <- pars$U
  h <- (U - L) / n

  b <- L + c(0:n) * h
  y <- 0.5 * (b[1:n] + b[2:(n + 1)])

  Fmat <- fy(
    y = y,
    x = y,
    pars = pars,
    h = h,
    disturbance = disturbance,
    disturbance_prev = disturbance_prev)

  Smat <- sx(
    x = y,
    pars = pars,
    disturbance = disturbance)

  Gmat <- matrix(0, n, n)
  Gmat[] <- t(
    outer(
      y,
      y,
      Vectorize(function(x, y) {
        gxy(
          x = x,
          y = y,
          pars = pars,
          disturbance = disturbance)
      }))) * h

  Tmat <- matrix(0, n, n)

  for (i in 1:(n / 2)) {
    Gmat[1, i] <- Gmat[1, i] + 1 - sum(Gmat[, i])
    Tmat[, i] <- Gmat[, i] * Smat[i]
  }

  for (i in (n / 2 + 1):n) {
    Gmat[n, i] <- Gmat[n, i] + 1 - sum(Gmat[, i])
    Tmat[, i] <- Gmat[, i] * Smat[i]
  }

  k_yx <- Fmat + Tmat

  list(
    k_yx = k_yx,
    Fmat = Fmat,
    Tmat = Tmat,
    Gmat = Gmat,
    Smat = Smat,
    meshpts = y,
    h = h)
}

lambda_ipm <- function(
    pars, disturbance = 0, disturbance_prev = 0) {
  K <- kernel(
    pars = pars,
    disturbance = disturbance,
    disturbance_prev = disturbance_prev)$k_yx

  Re(eigen(K, only.values = TRUE)$values[1])
}

6.11 Construct the mean observed initial size distribution

The initial vector is the arithmetic mean of annual size-frequency vectors. Unsized recruits are distributed over the fitted recruit-size distribution.

Code 
make_initial_n_mean <- function(pars, df_init = df) {
  n <- as.integer(pars$mat_siz)
  L <- pars$L
  U <- pars$U
  h <- (U - L) / n
  breaks <- seq(L, U, length.out = n + 1)
  b <- L + c(0:n) * h
  y <- 0.5 * (b[1:n] + b[2:(n + 1)])

  recruit_density <- recr_y(y, pars)
  recruit_density <- recruit_density /
    sum(recruit_density * h)

  years_i <- df_init %>%
    filter(!is.na(year)) %>%
    distinct(year) %>%
    arrange(year) %>%
    pull(year)

  counts_by_year <- purrr::map(years_i, function(year_i) {
    df_i <- df_init %>%
      filter(year == year_i)

    x <- df_i %>%
      filter(is.finite(logvol_t0)) %>%
      pull(logvol_t0)

    size_counts <- hist(
      pmin(pmax(x, L), U),
      breaks = breaks,
      plot = FALSE,
      include.lowest = TRUE)$counts

    n_unsized_recruits <- df_i %>%
      summarise(
        n = sum(
          !is.finite(logvol_t0) & recruits == 1,
          na.rm = TRUE)) %>%
      pull(n)

    size_counts +
      n_unsized_recruits * recruit_density * h
  })

  mean_counts <- Reduce(`+`, counts_by_year) /
    length(counts_by_year)

  mean_counts / h
}

6.13 Observed disturbance regime

Each unique quadrat-year receives equal weight. The four combinations preserve the distinction between current fire and fire in the previous year.

6.14 Build the state-specific and expected-regime kernels

Each state-specific kernel uses the flowering-stem reference corresponding to its previous-year-fire state. All components of the expected-regime kernel use the weighted reference stem abundance for the observed disturbance regime.

6.15 Calculate asymptotic and projected population growth

The asymptotic growth rate is the dominant eigenvalue of the kernel. The projected growth rate is the one-step change from the mean observed size distribution.

Code 
project_kernel <- function(K, pars, label, df_init = df) {
  n_obs <- make_initial_n_mean(pars, df_init)
  h <- (pars$U - pars$L) / pars$mat_siz
  n_initial <- sum(n_obs) * h

  n_proj <- K %*% n_obs
  n_projected <- sum(n_proj) * h

  tibble(
    lambda_type = label,
    asym_lambda = Re(
      eigen(
        K,
        only.values = TRUE)$values[1]),
    proj_lambda = n_projected / n_initial,
    n_initial = n_initial,
    n_projected = n_projected)
}

make_state_lambda <- function(
    K, pars, label, disturbance, disturbance_prev, p_state) {
  project_kernel(
    K = K,
    pars = pars,
    label = label) %>%
    mutate(
      disturbance = disturbance,
      disturbance_prev = disturbance_prev,
      observed_state_probability = p_state,
      flowering_stems_ref = pars$fs_ref,
      recruits_ref = predict_recruits_from_stems(
        flowering_stems = pars$fs_ref,
        pars = pars,
        disturbance = disturbance),
      recruits_per_stem = if_else(
        flowering_stems_ref > 0,
        recruits_ref / flowering_stems_ref,
        0))
}
Code

6.16 Observed annual abundance change in matched occupied quadrats

Counts include sized plants and recruits without a usable size measurement. Only quadrats with individual records in both consecutive years are retained. Historically sampled empty quadrats cannot be added because they have no individual rows in the workdata.

Code 
df_counts_quad_year <- df %>%
  filter(
    !is.na(site),
    !is.na(quad),
    !is.na(year)) %>%
  group_by(site, quad, year) %>%
  summarise(
    n_sized = sum(
      is.finite(logvol_t0),
      na.rm = TRUE),
    n_unsized_recruits = sum(
      !is.finite(logvol_t0) & recruits == 1,
      na.rm = TRUE),
    n_t0 = n_sized + n_unsized_recruits,
    .groups = 'drop') %>%
  arrange(site, quad, year) %>%
  group_by(site, quad) %>%
  mutate(
    year_t1 = lead(year),
    n_t1 = lead(n_t0),
    year_gap = year_t1 - year) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  filter(year_gap == 1)

df_obs_growth_year <- df_counts_quad_year %>%
  group_by(year) %>%
  summarise(
    n_t0 = sum(n_t0),
    n_t1 = sum(n_t1),
    n_quadrats = n(),
    n_sites = n_distinct(site),
    obs_lambda = n_t1 / n_t0,
    .groups = 'drop') %>%
  filter(n_t0 > 0)

    min(K_00),

    min(K_regime)),

    max(K_00),

    max(K_regime)),

    any(!is.finite(K_00)),

All kernel entries should be finite and non-negative. These checks must be repeated whenever the vital-rate models, mesh limits, recruitment conversion, or fire-state weighting are changed.

6.19 Interpretation of the mean model

The fitted model represents a fire-responsive perennial with a persistent seedbank. Current fire increases observed recruitment but can simultaneously reduce the performance of established plants. The strongest positive response occurs in the year following fire, when flowering and the resulting fertility contribution reflect previous-year disturbance.

The flowering-stem-to-recruit relationship is a quadrat-level relationship. Recruitment in quadrats without current flowering is attributed to the persistent seedbank. The negative flowering-stem relationship, especially in burned quadrats, is consistent with fewer open establishment sites where many productive adults are already present, while additional seed production may feed the seedbank instead of appearing immediately as recruits. This remains a phenomenological interpretation; the model does not identify parent plants or separate seed production, seed survival, germination, and establishment.

The expected-regime kernel combines the observed frequencies of the four fire states. It is therefore a deterministic summary of average demographic performance under the observed disturbance regime, not a stochastic fire model and not a simulation of a specific historical fire sequence.

The comparison with observed annual abundance change is useful but limited. The workdata contain individual records, so quadrats sampled with zero plants are absent from the historical series. The observed geometric mean therefore describes matched occupied quadrats and may omit some local extinction and recolonization events.

7 Mean IPM with one disturbance state for Polygala lewtonii

7.1 What this mean IPM does

This chapter develops the same deterministic mean integral projection model (IPM) for Polygala lewtonii as Chapter 9, but simplifies how fire is handled inside the IPM. The vital-rate models themselves are fitted exactly as before: survival and growth use current disturbance, flowering probability and flowering-stem number use previous-year disturbance, and quadrat-level recruitment uses current disturbance.

The change occurs only after the vital-rate models have been fitted and their coefficients have been extracted. From that point onward, the IPM uses one shared binary disturbance state for every demographic process. In other words, a kernel is either evaluated with disturbance = 0 for all vital rates or with disturbance = 1 for all vital rates. The coefficients fitted to disturbance_prev in the flowering models are therefore deliberately treated as if they belonged to the same disturbance level as the other vital rates.

The continuous state variable is log plant volume. For a plant of size \(z\) in year \(t\), the IPM projects the density of plant sizes in year \(t+1\) using a survival-growth component and a fertility component,

\[ K(z',z) = P(z',z) + F(z',z). \]

This simplified IPM therefore has only two disturbance-specific kernels:

  1. an undisturbed kernel, in which all vital rates receive disturbance = 0;
  2. a fire kernel, in which all vital rates receive disturbance = 1.

A third kernel averages these two kernels using the observed quadrat-year frequency of the shared disturbance variable. The model reports both the dominant eigenvalue of each kernel, which is the asymptotic population growth rate, and the one-step growth rate obtained by projecting the mean observed size distribution.

7.2 Main assumptions and interpretation

The model makes the following assumptions.

  1. Mean demographic relationships. Survival, growth, flowering, and recruitment relationships are pooled across years and sites. No year or site random effects are included. Year and site are retained only for data construction, disturbance timing, recruitment transitions, and validation.

  2. Annual and time-homogeneous transitions. Each kernel represents an annual transition under one fixed disturbance state. Within a disturbance state, the fitted vital-rate relationships are assumed not to change through time.

  3. The fitted disturbance timing is unchanged. Survival and growth are fitted with current disturbance, flowering probability and flowering-stem number are fitted with previous-year disturbance, and the flowering-stem-to- recruit model is fitted with current disturbance. No disturbance variable is changed in the model-fitting stage.

  4. One shared disturbance state in the IPM. After coefficient extraction, the distinction between current and previous-year disturbance is discarded. The same binary disturbance value is passed to survival, growth, flowering, flowering-stem production, and recruitment. This is a deliberate simplification for the IPM and should not be interpreted as preserving the observed timing of fire effects.

  5. Size is the continuous plant state. Individual heterogeneity other than size and disturbance exposure is not modeled explicitly.

  6. Phenomenological recruitment model. Total flowering stems in quadrat \(q\) during year \(t\) predict recruits in the same quadrat during year \(t+1\). Recruitment may occur when no flowering stems are recorded because the intercept represents emergence from the persistent seedbank. The negative flowering-stem coefficient, especially after fire, is interpreted as a possible density or establishment effect rather than as direct evidence of parent-specific fecundity.

  7. No explicit seedbank stage. The persistent seedbank is represented indirectly by the recruitment intercept and disturbance response. Predicted quadrat recruitment is converted to recruits per flowering stem at a quadrat-level reference stem abundance and allocated among plants according to expected flowering-stem production. This keeps the kernel linear but does not imply known parentage.

  8. Deterministic projection. The kernels do not include environmental stochasticity, demographic stochasticity, or parameter uncertainty.

  9. Observed two-state disturbance mixture. The expected-regime kernel uses the observed frequencies of disturbance = 0 and disturbance = 1 among quadrat-years as fixed weights. It no longer distinguishes current fire from previous-year fire inside the IPM.

  10. Mean initial size distribution. The one-step projected growth rate uses the arithmetic mean of annual observed size-frequency vectors. Recruits without a usable size measurement are distributed across the fitted recruit size distribution.

  11. Observed-growth validation is incomplete. Annual abundance change is calculated only from quadrats containing individual records in both consecutive years. Historically sampled but empty quadrats cannot be reconstructed consistently, so this comparison describes matched occupied quadrats rather than a complete census of all sampled quadrats.

The chapter retains the full model-fitting analysis from Chapter 9. Only the IPM-side disturbance handling is changed.

7.3 Set up the analysis

Code 
set.seed(100)
options(stringsAsFactors = FALSE)

7.3.1 Model specification

Code 
v_head <- 'archbold'
v_species <- 'Polygala lewtonii'
v_years_re <- c()

v_sp_abb <- tolower(
  gsub(
    ' ', '',
    paste(
      substr(unlist(strsplit(v_species, ' ')), 1, 2),
      collapse = '')))

v_script_prefix <- v_head
v_ggp_suffix <- paste(tools::toTitleCase(v_head), '-', v_species)

# Empty vectors select the best-supported polynomial by AICc.
v_mod_set_su <- c()
v_mod_set_gr <- c()
v_mod_set_fl <- c()
v_mod_set_fl_n <- c()
v_mod_set_re <- c()

7.4.1 Load the completed workdata

The workdata already contains current-year disturbance and disturbance in the exact previous year. These fields are retained directly rather than rebuilt from the subset of observed individual rows.

Code 
df <- read.csv(
  file.path(
    dir_data,
    paste0('ab_', v_sp_abb, '_df_workdata_260519.csv'))) %>%
  mutate(
    disturbance = as.numeric(dist_transition),
    disturbance_prev = as.numeric(disturbance_prev),
    year = as.integer(year),
    site = factor(site)) %>%
  filter(
    !is.na(year),
    !(year %in% v_years_re))

7.5 Construct the vital-rate data sets

7.5.1 Survival

Code 
df_su <- df %>%
  filter(
    !is.na(survives),
    size_t0 != 0,
    is.finite(logvol_t0),
    is.finite(logvol_t0_2),
    is.finite(logvol_t0_3),
    !is.na(disturbance)) %>%
  dplyr::select(
    id, site, year, size_t0, survives, size_t1,
    logsize_t0, logsize_t1, logsize_t0_2, logsize_t0_3,
    volume_t0, volume_t1, logvol_t0, logvol_t1,
    logvol_t0_2, logvol_t0_3, disturbance, stage)

7.5.2 Growth

Code 
df_gr <- df %>%
  filter(
    size_t0 != 0,
    size_t1 != 0,
    is.finite(logvol_t0),
    is.finite(logvol_t1),
    is.finite(logvol_t0_2),
    is.finite(logvol_t0_3),
    !is.na(disturbance)) %>%
  dplyr::select(
    id, site, year, size_t0, size_t1,
    logsize_t0, logsize_t1, logsize_t0_2, logsize_t0_3,

    logvol_t0_2, logvol_t0_3, disturbance, stage)

7.5.3 Flowering probability and flowering-stem number

Observed recruits are retained because some recruits flowered.

Code 
df_fl <- df %>%
  filter(
    !is.na(flower),
    is.finite(logvol_t0),
    is.finite(logvol_t0_2),
    is.finite(logvol_t0_3),
    !is.na(disturbance_prev)) %>%
  dplyr::select(
    id, site, year, size_t0, flower, fl_nr, size_t1,
    logsize_t0, logsize_t1, logsize_t0_2, logsize_t0_3,
    volume_t0, volume_t1, logvol_t0, logvol_t1,
    logvol_t0_2, logvol_t0_3, disturbance_prev, stage, recruits)

df_fl_cond <- df_fl %>%
  filter(
    flower == 1,
    !is.na(fl_nr),
    fl_nr > 0,
    fl_nr == round(fl_nr))

7.5.4 Quadrat-level flowering stems and recruits

Total flowering stems in quadrat \(q\) during year \(t\) predict recruits in the same quadrat during year \(t+1\). A quadrat transition is retained only when the same quadrat has individual records in both years.

Code 
df_quad_year_sampled <- df %>%
  distinct(site, quad, year)

df_fs2r <- df %>%
  group_by(site, quad, year) %>%
  summarise(
    fs_t0 = sum(fl_nr, na.rm = TRUE),
    disturbance = if_else(
      all(is.na(disturbance)),
      NA_real_,
      max(disturbance, na.rm = TRUE)),
    .groups = 'drop') %>%
  mutate(
    year_t1 = year + 1) %>%
  semi_join(
    df_quad_year_sampled %>%
      transmute(
        site,
        quad,
        year_t1 = year),
    by = c(
      'site',
      'quad',
      'year_t1')) %>%
  left_join(
    df %>%
      filter(recruits == 1) %>%
      count(
        site,
        quad,
        year,
        name = 're_t1'),
    by = c(
      'site',
      'quad',
      'year_t1' = 'year')) %>%
  mutate(
    re_t1 = replace_na(re_t1, 0L),
    site = factor(site),
    fs_t0_log = log1p(fs_t0),
    re_t1_log = log1p(re_t1)) %>%
  filter(
    !is.na(year),
    !is.na(year_t1),
    !is.na(disturbance),
    !(year %in% v_years_re),
    !(year_t1 %in% v_years_re))

df_fs2r %>%
  summarise(
    quadrats = n_distinct(quad),
    transitions = n(),
    zero_stems = sum(fs_t0 == 0),
    zero_recruits = sum(re_t1 == 0),
    burned_transitions = sum(disturbance == 1),
    unburned_transitions = sum(disturbance == 0))

7.6 Fit the mean vital-rate models

Candidate models use intercept-only, fire-only, and first- through third-order size polynomials, each with and without the relevant fire term. Empty model-set vectors select the model with the lowest AICc.

7.6.1 Survival model

Code 
mod_su_00 <- glm(
  survives ~ 1,
  data = df_su,
  family = binomial)

mod_su_0 <- glm(
  survives ~ disturbance,
  data = df_su,
  family = binomial)

mod_su_10 <- glm(
  survives ~ logvol_t0,
  data = df_su,
  family = binomial)

mod_su_1 <- glm(
  survives ~ logvol_t0 + disturbance,
  data = df_su,
  family = binomial)

mod_su_20 <- glm(
  survives ~ logvol_t0 + logvol_t0_2,
  data = df_su,
  family = binomial)

mod_su_2 <- glm(
  survives ~ logvol_t0 + logvol_t0_2 + disturbance,
  data = df_su,
  family = binomial)

mod_su_30 <- glm(
  survives ~ logvol_t0 + logvol_t0_2 + logvol_t0_3,
  data = df_su,
  family = binomial)

mod_su_3 <- glm(
  survives ~ logvol_t0 + logvol_t0_2 + logvol_t0_3 +
    disturbance,
  data = df_su,
  family = binomial)

mods_su <- list(
  mod_su_00, mod_su_0, mod_su_10, mod_su_1,
  mod_su_20, mod_su_2, mod_su_30, mod_su_3)

mods_su_dAICc <- bbmle::AICctab(
  mods_su,
  weights = TRUE,
  sort = FALSE)$dAICc

mods_su_sorted <- order(mods_su_dAICc)

if (length(v_mod_set_su) == 0) {
  mod_su_index_best <- mods_su_sorted[1]
} else {
  mod_su_index_best <- v_mod_set_su + 1
}

v_mod_su_index <- floor((mod_su_index_best - 1) / 2)
mod_su_best <- mods_su[[mod_su_index_best]]

summary(mod_su_best)

7.6.3 Growth variance

Growth variance is modeled as an exponential function of the fitted growth mean.

Code 
mod_gr_x <- fitted(mod_gr_best)
mod_gr_y <- resid(mod_gr_best)^2

mod_gr_var <- nls(
  mod_gr_y ~ a * exp(b * mod_gr_x),
  start = list(a = 1, b = 0),
  control = nls.control(
    maxiter = 1000,
    tol = 1e-6,
    warnOnly = TRUE))

7.6.6 Flowering-stem-to-recruit model

The recruitment candidates allow a seedbank intercept, a current-fire effect, a flowering-stem effect, and their interaction. No year or site random effects are fitted.

Code

  re_t1_log ~ 1,
  data = df_fs2r)

mod_re_0 <- lm(
  re_t1_log ~ disturbance,
  data = df_fs2r)

mod_re_10 <- lm(
  re_t1_log ~ fs_t0_log,
  data = df_fs2r)

mod_re_1 <- lm(
  re_t1_log ~ fs_t0_log + disturbance,
  data = df_fs2r)

mod_re_20 <- lm(
  re_t1_log ~ fs_t0_log * disturbance,
  data = df_fs2r)

mods_re <- list(
  mod_re_00,
  mod_re_0,
  mod_re_10,
  mod_re_1,
  mod_re_20)

mods_re_dAICc <- bbmle::AICctab(
  mods_re,
  weights = TRUE,
  sort = FALSE)$dAICc

mods_re_sorted <- order(mods_re_dAICc)

if (length(v_mod_set_re) == 0) {
  mod_re_index_best <- mods_re_sorted[1]
} else {
  mod_re_index_best <- v_mod_set_re + 1
}

v_mod_re_index <- mod_re_index_best - 1

Code 
df_recruit_model_support <- tibble(
  model = c(
    'Intercept only',

  dAICc = as.numeric(mods_re_dAICc)) %>%
  mutate(
    weight = exp(-0.5 * dAICc) /
      sum(exp(-0.5 * dAICc))) %>%
  arrange(dAICc)

(#tab:mean-ipm-dist1-recruitment-support)AICc support for quadrat-level flowering-stem-to-recruit models.
model dAICc weight
Full interaction 0.00 0.569
Disturbance only 1.56 0.260
Flowering stems + disturbance 2.40 0.171
Intercept only 52.77 0.000
Flowering stems 53.63 0.000

The full interaction model is selected. Its fitted form is

\[ \log(1 + R_{q,t+1}) = \beta_0 + \beta_1\log(1 + M_{q,t}) + \beta_d d_{q,t} + \beta_{1d}\log(1 + M_{q,t})d_{q,t} + \varepsilon, \]

where \(M_{q,t}\) is total flowering stems, \(R_{q,t+1}\) is the number of recruits in the same quadrat in the following year, and \(d_{q,t}\) indicates current fire.

7.6.8 Recruitment slopes and uncertainty

Code 
re_coef <- coef(mod_re_20)
re_vcov <- vcov(mod_re_20)

slope_unburned <- re_coef['fs_t0_log']

se_unburned <- sqrt(
  re_vcov[
    'fs_t0_log',
    'fs_t0_log'])

slope_burned <-
  re_coef['fs_t0_log'] +
  re_coef['fs_t0_log:disturbance']

se_burned <- sqrt(
  re_vcov[
    'fs_t0_log',
    'fs_t0_log'] +
  re_vcov[
    'fs_t0_log:disturbance',
    'fs_t0_log:disturbance'] +
  2 * re_vcov[
    'fs_t0_log',
    'fs_t0_log:disturbance'])

df_recruit_slopes <- tibble(
  disturbance = c(0, 1),
  slope = c(
    slope_unburned,
    slope_burned),
  lower_95 = c(
    slope_unburned - 1.96 * se_unburned,
    slope_burned - 1.96 * se_burned),
  upper_95 = c(
    slope_unburned + 1.96 * se_unburned,
    slope_burned + 1.96 * se_burned))

7.7 Plot the selected vital-rate models

Code 
make_mean_prediction <- function(data, model, disturbance_var) {
  x <- seq(
    min(data$logvol_t0, na.rm = TRUE),
    max(data$logvol_t0, na.rm = TRUE),
    length.out = 200)

  pred <- expand_grid(
    logvol_t0 = x,
    disturbance_value = c(0, 1)) %>%
    mutate(
      logvol_t0_2 = logvol_t0^2,
      logvol_t0_3 = logvol_t0^3,
      disturbance_plot = factor(
        disturbance_value,
        levels = c(0, 1),
        labels = c('No fire', 'Fire')))

  pred[[disturbance_var]] <- pred$disturbance_value
  pred$prediction <- predict(
    model,
    newdata = pred,
    type = 'response')

  pred
}

make_mean_plot <- function(
    data, model, response, disturbance_var, title, y_lab,
    probability = FALSE) {
  pred <- make_mean_prediction(
    data = data,
    model = model,
    disturbance_var = disturbance_var)

  data_plot <- data %>%
    mutate(
      disturbance_plot = factor(
        .data[[disturbance_var]],
        levels = c(0, 1),
        labels = c('No fire', 'Fire')))

  point_layer <- if (probability) {
    geom_jitter(
      data = data_plot,
      aes(
        x = logvol_t0,
        y = .data[[response]],
        color = disturbance_plot),
      alpha = 0.15,
      size = 0.7,
      width = 0.05,
      height = 0.05)
  } else {
    geom_point(
      data = data_plot,
      aes(
        x = logvol_t0,
        y = .data[[response]],
        color = disturbance_plot),
      alpha = 0.15,
      size = 0.7)
  }

  p <- ggplot() +
    point_layer +
    geom_line(
      data = pred,
      aes(
        x = logvol_t0,
        y = prediction,
        color = disturbance_plot),
      linewidth = 0.8) +
    scale_color_manual(
      values = c(
        'No fire' = 'black',
        'Fire' = 'red')) +
    theme_bw() +
    labs(
      title = title,
      subtitle = v_ggp_suffix,
      x = expression('log(volume)'[t0]),
      y = y_lab,
      color = NULL)

  if (probability) {
    p <- p + coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, 1))
  }

  p
}

7.9 Extract the selected model parameters

The extraction functions return zero for terms that are absent from the selected model. The same IPM functions can therefore use any selected candidate without manual coefficient changes.

Code 
size_term_map <- c(
  b0 = '(Intercept)',
  b1 = 'logvol_t0',
  b2 = 'logvol_t0_2',
  b3 = 'logvol_t0_3',
  bd = 'disturbance')

lagged_size_term_map <- c(
  b0 = '(Intercept)',
  b1 = 'logvol_t0',
  b2 = 'logvol_t0_2',
  b3 = 'logvol_t0_3',
  bd = 'disturbance_prev')

extract_terms <- function(model, prefix, term_map) {
  coefs <- stats::coef(model)

  values <- vapply(term_map, function(term_i) {
    if (term_i %in% names(coefs)) {
      unname(coefs[[term_i]])
    } else {
      0
    }
  }, numeric(1))

  names(values) <- paste0(prefix, names(term_map))
  values
}

extract_coef <- function(model, term, default = 0) {
  coefs <- stats::coef(model)

  if (term %in% names(coefs)) {
    unname(coefs[[term]])
  } else {
    default
  }
}

grow_var_coef <- stats::coef(mod_gr_var)

  c(
    df_gr$logvol_t0,
    df_gr$logvol_t1,

  na.rm = TRUE,

7.10 Define the IPM functions

The extracted flowering coefficients still come from models fitted with disturbance_prev. From this point onward, however, their disturbance coefficient is used with the same generic disturbance argument as all other vital rates.

7.10.1 General parameter and linear-predictor functions

Code 
get_par <- function(pars, par_name, default = 0) {
  if (!is.null(pars[[par_name]])) {
    pars[[par_name]]
  } else {
    default
  }
}

vital_lp <- function(x, pars, prefix, disturbance = 0) {
  get_par(pars, paste0(prefix, 'b0')) +
    get_par(pars, paste0(prefix, 'b1')) * x +
    get_par(pars, paste0(prefix, 'b2')) * x^2 +
    get_par(pars, paste0(prefix, 'b3')) * x^3 +
    get_par(pars, paste0(prefix, 'bd')) * disturbance
}

7.10.2 Survival

Code 
sx <- function(x, pars, disturbance = 0) {
  plogis(vital_lp(
    x = x,
    pars = pars,
    prefix = 'surv_',
    disturbance = disturbance))
}

7.10.3 Growth

Code 
grow_mu <- function(x, pars, disturbance = 0) {
  vital_lp(
    x = x,
    pars = pars,
    prefix = 'grow_',
    disturbance = disturbance)
}

grow_sd <- function(mean_value, pars) {
  variance <- get_par(pars, 'grow_var_a') *
    exp(get_par(pars, 'grow_var_b') * mean_value)

  sqrt(pmax(variance, .Machine$double.eps))
}

gxy <- function(x, y, pars, disturbance = 0) {
  mean_value <- grow_mu(
    x = x,
    pars = pars,
    disturbance = disturbance)

  sd_value <- grow_sd(
    mean_value = mean_value,
    pars = pars)

  dnorm(
    y,
    mean = mean_value,
    sd = sd_value)
}

7.10.4 Flowering probability and conditional flowering-stem number

The fitted flowering models still use disturbance_prev; only their IPM functions are changed so that the extracted disturbance coefficient is driven by the shared disturbance state.

Code 
fl_x <- function(x, pars, disturbance = 0) {
  plogis(vital_lp(
    x = x,
    pars = pars,
    prefix = 'fl_',
    disturbance = disturbance))
}

fln_x <- function(x, pars, disturbance = 0) {
  exp(vital_lp(
    x = x,
    pars = pars,
    prefix = 'fln_',
    disturbance = disturbance))
}

fs_x <- function(x, pars, disturbance = 0) {
  fl_x(
    x = x,
    pars = pars,
    disturbance = disturbance) *
    fln_x(
      x = x,
      pars = pars,
      disturbance = disturbance)
}

7.10.5 Flowering-stem-to-recruit conversion

The coefficient extraction supports intercept-only, disturbance-only, flowering-stem, additive, and interaction models. Recruitment is not forced to zero when flowering stems equal zero because the fitted intercept represents seedbank emergence.

Code 
predict_recruits_from_stems <- function(
    flowering_stems, pars, disturbance = 0) {
  stems_nonnegative <- pmax(flowering_stems, 0)

  slope <- get_par(pars, 're_b1') +
    get_par(pars, 're_bf') * disturbance

  eta <- get_par(pars, 're_b0') +
    get_par(pars, 're_bd') * disturbance +
    slope * log1p(stems_nonnegative)

  recruits <- expm1(
    eta + 0.5 * get_par(pars, 're_sigma')^2)

  pmax(recruits, 0)
}

recruits_per_stem <- function(pars, disturbance = 0) {
  fs_ref <- get_par(pars, 'fs_ref', 0)

  if (!is.finite(fs_ref) || fs_ref <= 0) {
    return(0)
  }

  predict_recruits_from_stems(
    flowering_stems = fs_ref,
    pars = pars,
    disturbance = disturbance) / fs_ref
}

rx <- function(x, pars, disturbance = 0) {
  fs_x(
    x = x,
    pars = pars,
    disturbance = disturbance) *
    recruits_per_stem(
      pars = pars,
      disturbance = disturbance)
}

The fitted model predicts nonzero recruitment from the seedbank when no current flowering stems are recorded.

7.10.6 Recruit size distribution and fertility matrix

Code 
recr_y <- function(y, pars) {
  dnorm(
    y,
    mean = get_par(pars, 'recr_mean'),
    sd = get_par(pars, 'recr_sd'))
}

fy <- function(y, x, pars, h, disturbance = 0) {
  Pvec <- recr_y(y, pars)
  recruit_mass <- sum(Pvec * h)

  if (!is.finite(recruit_mass) || recruit_mass <= 0) {
    stop('Recruit size distribution has no mass inside the mesh')
  }

  Pvec <- Pvec / recruit_mass

  Rvec <- rx(
    x = x,
    pars = pars,
    disturbance = disturbance)

  outer(Pvec, Rvec) * h
}

7.10.7 Full kernel

Only one disturbance argument is now accepted by the fertility and full-kernel functions. That value is propagated to every vital-rate component.

Code 
kernel <- function(pars, disturbance = 0) {
  n <- as.integer(pars$mat_siz)
  L <- pars$L
  U <- pars$U
  h <- (U - L) / n

  b <- L + c(0:n) * h
  y <- 0.5 * (b[1:n] + b[2:(n + 1)])

  Fmat <- fy(
    y = y,
    x = y,
    pars = pars,
    h = h,
    disturbance = disturbance)

  Smat <- sx(
    x = y,
    pars = pars,
    disturbance = disturbance)

  Gmat <- matrix(0, n, n)
  Gmat[] <- t(
    outer(
      y,
      y,
      Vectorize(function(x, y) {
        gxy(
          x = x,
          y = y,
          pars = pars,
          disturbance = disturbance)
      }))) * h

  Tmat <- matrix(0, n, n)

  for (i in 1:(n / 2)) {
    Gmat[1, i] <- Gmat[1, i] + 1 - sum(Gmat[, i])
    Tmat[, i] <- Gmat[, i] * Smat[i]
  }

  for (i in (n / 2 + 1):n) {
    Gmat[n, i] <- Gmat[n, i] + 1 - sum(Gmat[, i])
    Tmat[, i] <- Gmat[, i] * Smat[i]
  }

  k_yx <- Fmat + Tmat

  list(
    k_yx = k_yx,
    Fmat = Fmat,
    Tmat = Tmat,
    Gmat = Gmat,
    Smat = Smat,
    meshpts = y,
    h = h)
}

lambda_ipm <- function(pars, disturbance = 0) {
  K <- kernel(
    pars = pars,
    disturbance = disturbance)$k_yx

  Re(eigen(K, only.values = TRUE)$values[1])
}

7.11 Construct the mean observed initial size distribution

The initial vector is the arithmetic mean of annual size-frequency vectors. Unsized recruits are distributed over the fitted recruit-size distribution.

Code 
make_initial_n_mean <- function(pars, df_init = df) {
  n <- as.integer(pars$mat_siz)
  L <- pars$L
  U <- pars$U
  h <- (U - L) / n
  breaks <- seq(L, U, length.out = n + 1)
  b <- L + c(0:n) * h
  y <- 0.5 * (b[1:n] + b[2:(n + 1)])

  recruit_density <- recr_y(y, pars)
  recruit_density <- recruit_density /
    sum(recruit_density * h)

  years_i <- df_init %>%
    filter(!is.na(year)) %>%
    distinct(year) %>%
    arrange(year) %>%
    pull(year)

  counts_by_year <- purrr::map(years_i, function(year_i) {
    df_i <- df_init %>%
      filter(year == year_i)

    x <- df_i %>%
      filter(is.finite(logvol_t0)) %>%
      pull(logvol_t0)

    size_counts <- hist(
      pmin(pmax(x, L), U),
      breaks = breaks,
      plot = FALSE,
      include.lowest = TRUE)$counts

    n_unsized_recruits <- df_i %>%
      summarise(
        n = sum(
          !is.finite(logvol_t0) & recruits == 1,
          na.rm = TRUE)) %>%
      pull(n)

    size_counts +
      n_unsized_recruits * recruit_density * h
  })

  mean_counts <- Reduce(`+`, counts_by_year) /
    length(counts_by_year)

  mean_counts / h
}

7.14 Build the state-specific and expected-regime kernels

The IPM now has only an undisturbed and a fire kernel. In each kernel, the same disturbance value is supplied to every vital-rate function. The expected-regime kernel is their observed-frequency-weighted average.

Code 
pars_0 <- pars_mean
pars_0$fs_ref <- mean_stems_no_fire

pars_1 <- pars_mean
pars_1$fs_ref <- mean_stems_fire

# All mixture components use the same expected total flowering-stem production
# under the observed disturbance regime.
pars_regime <- pars_mean
pars_regime$fs_ref <- mean_stems_regime

K_0 <- kernel(
  pars = pars_0,
  disturbance = 0)$k_yx

K_1 <- kernel(
  pars = pars_1,
  disturbance = 1)$k_yx

K_regime_0 <- kernel(
  pars = pars_regime,
  disturbance = 0)$k_yx

K_regime_1 <- kernel(
  pars = pars_regime,
  disturbance = 1)$k_yx

K_regime <-
  p_0 * K_regime_0 +
  p_1 * K_regime_1

7.15 Calculate asymptotic and projected population growth

The asymptotic growth rate is the dominant eigenvalue of the kernel. The projected growth rate is the one-step change from the mean observed size distribution.

Code 
project_kernel <- function(K, pars, label, df_init = df) {
  n_obs <- make_initial_n_mean(pars, df_init)
  h <- (pars$U - pars$L) / pars$mat_siz
  n_initial <- sum(n_obs) * h

  n_proj <- K %*% n_obs
  n_projected <- sum(n_proj) * h

  tibble(
    lambda_type = label,
    asym_lambda = Re(
      eigen(
        K,
        only.values = TRUE)$values[1]),
    proj_lambda = n_projected / n_initial,
    n_initial = n_initial,
    n_projected = n_projected)
}

make_state_lambda <- function(
    K, pars, label, disturbance, p_state) {
  project_kernel(
    K = K,
    pars = pars,
    label = label) %>%
    mutate(
      disturbance = disturbance,
      observed_state_probability = p_state,
      flowering_stems_ref = pars$fs_ref,
      recruits_ref = predict_recruits_from_stems(
        flowering_stems = pars$fs_ref,
        pars = pars,
        disturbance = disturbance),
      recruits_per_stem = if_else(
        flowering_stems_ref > 0,
        recruits_ref / flowering_stems_ref,
        0))
}
Code

  make_state_lambda(
    K = K_1,
    pars = pars_1,

  p_1 * predict_recruits_from_stems(

df_lambda_regime <- project_kernel(

7.19 Interpretation of the mean model

The fitted vital-rate models retain the same biological timing as in Chapter 9: current disturbance affects survival, growth, and the quadrat-level recruitment model, whereas previous-year disturbance affects flowering probability and flowering-stem number. The simplification introduced here begins only when those fitted coefficients are assembled into the IPM.

Inside the IPM, a single binary disturbance state is imposed on all demographic processes simultaneously. Consequently, the Fire kernel should be interpreted as a deliberately aligned disturbance scenario, not as a literal annual fire transition supported by the original timing of every vital rate. In particular, the flowering disturbance coefficients were estimated from previous-year fire but are evaluated at the same shared state as current-fire effects in the other vital rates.

The flowering-stem-to-recruit relationship remains a quadrat-level relationship. Recruitment in quadrats without current flowering is attributed to the persistent seedbank. The model does not identify parent plants or separate seed production, seed survival, germination, and establishment.

The expected-regime kernel combines the observed frequencies of the two shared disturbance states. It is therefore a deterministic summary under this imposed two-state disturbance representation, not a stochastic fire model and not a simulation of the historical sequence of current and previous-year fire.

The comparison with observed annual abundance change is unchanged from Chapter 9 and remains limited by the available workdata. Quadrats sampled with zero plants are absent from the historical individual-level series, so the observed geometric mean describes matched occupied quadrats and may omit some local extinction and recolonization events.

8 Historical integral projection models

8.1 Background

Standard integral projection models (IPMs) describe changes in a continuously structured population between consecutive time steps. If \(x\) denotes individual size at time \(t\) and \(y\) denotes size at time \(t+1\), population projection can be written as

\[ n(y,t+1) = \int_L^U K(y,x)n(x,t)\,dx, \]

where the projection kernel is commonly separated into a survival-growth component, \(P(y,x)\), and a fecundity component, \(F(y,x)\):

\[ K(y,x) = P(y,x) + F(y,x). \]

After discretizing the continuous size distribution into \(m\) mesh points, this becomes the familiar matrix projection

\[ \mathbf{n}_{t+1} = \mathbf{K}\mathbf{n}_t, \]

with

\[ \mathbf{K} = \mathbf{P}+\mathbf{F}. \]

An important assumption of this standard, or ahistorical, formulation is that the demographic future of an individual is completely described by its state at time \(t\). Conditional on current size, information from earlier time steps is not retained. Thus, two individuals of equal size at time \(t\) are treated as demographically equivalent even if they reached that size through different histories.

Historical population models relax this assumption. Previous states or events may influence demographic performance after accounting for current state (Ehrlén 2000; Shefferson et al. 2021). In a general second-order historical model, demographic transitions can therefore depend on the sequence

\[ z_{t-1} \rightarrow z_t \rightarrow z_{t+1}, \]

rather than only on

\[ z_t \rightarrow z_{t+1}. \]

The relevant history need not necessarily be previous individual size. It may also represent previous reproductive status, damage, resource allocation, or environmental conditions that produce carry-over effects.

Here, two different historical formulations are considered. The first is the time-lagged IPM of Kuss et al. (2008), in which fecundity operates with an additional one-year delay. The second is an environmental historical IPM in which the population retains information about fire during the previous interval because different demographic processes respond to fire over different time periods.

Although both approaches enlarge the population state and produce a megamatrix, the biological meaning of the additional state differs between them.

8.2 Readings

Kuss, P., Rees, M., Ægisdóttir, H. H., Ellner, S. P., & Stöcklin, J. (2008). Evolutionary demography of long‐lived monocarpic perennials: a time‐lagged integral projection model. Journal of Ecology, 96(4), 821-832.

  1. “So far, the existing class of models assume that demographic rates are only influenced by current individual state, say size and/or age. In many species, however, the decision to flower is made many months (e.g. Agave deserti; Tissue & Nobel 1990) or years (Frasera speciosa; Taylor & Inouye 1985) before flowering occurs. Additionally, flowering individuals of monocarpic perennials often have a different morphology, for example, withered or absent rosette leaves, such that size measurements in the year of flowering cannot be compared with the years prior to flowering (e.g. Campanula sibirica, C. spicata; Hegi 1975). In these latter cases, an additional time-lag needs to be incorporated into the models in order to faithfully represent the demography of a study species.”

  2. “Our objectives in this study are therefore (i) to present a theoretical and computational framework for a time-lagged IPM which allows demographic transitions to depend on an individual’s state either in the current year or the year before, (ii) to demonstrate that the novel combination of field methods (permanent plots and herb chronology) can be used to parameterize efficiently and validate IPMs with data from the long-lived monocarpic C. thyrsoides collected from a relatively short census period, (iii) to use the model to predict the age-structure observed in the field and determine the evolutionarily stable flowering strategy, and (iv) to draw general conclusions about the evolution of the flowering strategies in long-lived vs. short-lived monocarpic plant species.”

  3. “However, in many species a complication arises because either (i) rosette size cannot be measured in the year the plants flower or (ii) the decision to flower is made the year before plants flower. As a consequence the probability of flowering and seed production in year t has to be predicted as a function of plant size in year t − 1, and any seedlings produced then enter the population in year t + 1. Therefore the time-lagged IPM becomes”

  4. “The matrix K is useful for calculating various measures of population growth; however, it is inappropriate for sensitivity and elasticity analyses because the identity matrix, I, in the lower left hand corner is simply a computational device and not a biological transition.”

Ehrlén, J. (2000). The dynamics of plant populations: does the history of individuals matter?. Ecology, 81(6), 1675-1684.

  1. “At the level of individuals, historical effects in which past conditions influence future performance are particularly likely to occur in long-lived organisms that store resources between seasons and that form organs months or years before their elaboration. Such carry-over mechanisms have been documented in several perennial plant species, but the implications for population processes are poorly known. In this study, I examine how the history of individuals influences their future performance, population dynamics, and life cycle structure in the long-lived herb Lathyrus vernus. Overall effects of plant history on population dynamics, in terms of growth rate, reproductive values, stable stage distribution, and elasticities, are examined by comparing an ordinary first-order matrix model with a second-order matrix model. In the latter, not only the present state of individuals, but also their past state is allowed to influence future fate.”

  2. “In perennial plants, the current phenotype of an individual and its response to environmental change have been shown to reflect the individual’s history, i.e., its past phenotype and environment (Primack and Hall 1990, Bullock et al. 1993, Geber et al. 1997). Such carry-over mechanisms imply that the performance of individuals can be influenced both by past environmental conditions, such as herbivory or abiotic factors (Taylor and Inouye 1985, Nobel 1987, Bullock et al. 1993, 1995, Crone 1997, Rose et al. 1998), and by past internal plant events such as morphological development and resource allocation patterns (Karlsson 1986, Karlsson et al. 1990, Primack and Hall 1990, Geber et al. 1997). The mechanisms by which past events can influence plant phenotypes and their ability to respond to environmental variation include resource storage and a temporal separation between organ formation and elaboration. Resource stores are widely recognized as important to the ecology of perennial plants (Chapin et al. 1990), and organ preformation is widespread among angiosperms (Geber et al. 1997). Hence, carry-over mechanisms and historical effects are likely to occur in many perennial plant species.”

  3. “There are several ways in which historical events may influence the future performance of plants that currently belong to the same stage. Such historical effects may arise because the costs of allocating resources to one function, e.g., reproduction, in terms of decreased allocation to other functions, are not expressed until after more than one year (e.g., Primack and Hall 1990). Moreover, in plants that have the potential to accumulate resources and store them among seasons, plant size may be partly restored after it has been depressed during one season, e.g., by herbivory. In addition, correlations between past and current performance can be mediated by the external environment. If size changes of individuals reflect altered environmental conditions that persist for more than one season, then individuals experiencing a certain size change during one year are likely to experience a similar change during the next year.”

  4. “Conventional matrix models are first-order models, i.e., the stage distribution at time t + 1 depends solely on the stage distribution at time t.[…] When the Markovian process is extended to be second order, the stage distribution at time t + 1 becomes dependent upon the distribution at time t − 1 as well as that at time t, and on second-order transition probabilities (Tanner et al. 1996). The matrix of transition probabilities in a second-order model is no longer two-dimensional, but instead becomes three-dimensional. In analogy with the conventional notation, the equation for the system can be expressed as: x(t + 1, t) = Ax(t, t − 1), where A is the three-dimensional transition probability matrix and x(t + 1, t) is a two-dimensional matrix describing the joint stage distributions at times t + 1 and t. Thus, the element aijk of A represents the probability that an individual of stages k and j in years t − 1 and t, respectively, transitions to stages j and i in years t and t + 1.”

  5. “In ‘historical’ models, each transition from year t to year t + 1 was calculated separately for the seven stages of individuals in year t − 1 (Table 2). To allow for the analytical procedures developed for first-order models, three-dimensional matrices can be converted to a two-dimensional form and two-dimensional stage vectors can be transformed into an one-dimensional form. In this two-dimensional matrix, the columns represent the combinations of individual stages in years t − 1 and t (j, k), and rows represent the combination of individual stages in years t and t + 1 (i, j). Hence, the three-dimensional matrix for L. vernus was converted to a two-dimensional form, including transitions from all combinations of stage year t − 1 and year t to all combinations of stage year t and stage year t + 1.”

Shefferson, R. P., Kurokawa, S., & Ehrlén, J. (2021). lefko3: Analysing individual history through size‐classified matrix population models. Methods in Ecology and Evolution, 12(2), 378-382.

  1. “Matrix projection models typically assume that the histories of individuals do not influence population dynamics. Specifically, the state of an individual in time t + 1 is solely dependent on the state of that individual at time t. We refer to such MPMs as ahistorical MPMs, or ahMPMs, and use the term MPM to refer generally to any kind of MPM. This assumption is a temporal interpretation of the assumption of independence and identical distribution (iid) in vital rates, and it allows the creation of low-dimension MPMs in which columns represent life-history stage (or age) in time t and rows represent stage (or age) in time t + 1 (Caswell, 2001). When stage-based MPMs are characterized by transitions between life-history stages, yielding a matrix in which the transition probabilities and fecundity of an individual in time t + 1 are governed solely by its condition in time t (Lefkovitch, 1965). Integral projection models (IPMs) are function-based MPMs in which size follows a Gaussian distribution (Ellner & Rees, 2006). Neither traditional MPMs nor IPMs incorporate individual history.”

  2. “Matrix projection models typically assume that the histories of individuals do not influence population dynamics. Specifically, the state of an individual in time t + 1 is solely dependent on the state of that individual at time t. We refer to such MPMs as ahistorical MPMs, or ahMPMs, and use the term MPM to refer generally to any kind of MPM. This assumption is a temporal interpretation of the assumption of independence and identical distribution (iid) in vital rates, and it allows the creation of low-dimension MPMs in which columns represent life-history stage (or age) in time t and rows represent stage (or age) in time t + 1 (Caswell, 2001). When stage-based MPMs are characterized by transitions between life-history stages, yielding a matrix in which the transition probabilities and fecundity of an individual in time t + 1 are governed solely by its condition in time t (Lefkovitch, 1965). Integral projection models (IPMs) are function-based MPMs in which size follows a Gaussian distribution (Ellner & Rees, 2006). Neither traditional MPMs nor IPMs incorporate individual history.”

  3. “In an ahMPM, rows and columns correspond to the states of individuals in times t and t + 1 (Table 1a). hMPMs add time t − 1 into the two-dimensional matrix by recharacterizing the rows and columns of the matrix so that they correspond to stage-pairs defined across two consecutive times (Table 1b). Redefining stages in this way leads to large, sparse matrices. An ahMPM with m stages will have m2 elements, all of which may be non-zero. A hMPM with m stages will have m2 stage-pairs on each axis and m4 elements, of which m3 elements are potentially estimable and (m − 1)m3 elements are structural zeroes. Structural zeroes result from the fact that row stage pairs and column stage pairs both include stage in time t, and so stage at time t must be equal in both for a transition to be estimable.”

  4. “Function modelsearch() takes historical vertical datasets and estimates historical and ahistorical linear models of all necessary vital rates to create function-based MPMs, including complex IPMs.[…] Historical global models can include size and reproductive status in times t and t − 1 and their interactions.”

8.3 Time-lagged IPM

Kuss et al. (2008) developed a time-lagged IPM for a demographic system in which reproduction could not be related to individual size in the same year. Survival and growth were determined by size at time \(t\), whereas reproduction contributing to the population at \(t+1\) depended on size at \(t-1\).

Kuss et al. (2008): “demographic transitions to depend on an individual’s state either in the current year or the year before”

The resulting population projection is

\[ \mathbf{n}_{t+1} = \mathbf{P}\mathbf{n}_t + \mathbf{F}\mathbf{n}_{t-1}. \]

The state of the system must therefore contain both the current and previous population vectors:

\[ \mathbf{N}_t = \begin{pmatrix} \mathbf{n}_t \\ \mathbf{n}_{t-1} \end{pmatrix}. \]

Projection can then be written as

\[ \begin{pmatrix} \mathbf{n}_{t+1} \\ \mathbf{n}_t \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} \mathbf{P} & \mathbf{F} \\ \mathbf{I} & \mathbf{0} \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} \mathbf{n}_t \\ \mathbf{n}_{t-1} \end{pmatrix}. \]

Thus, the historical projection matrix is

\[ \mathbf{K}_{\mathrm{lag}} = \begin{pmatrix} \mathbf{P} & \mathbf{F} \\ \mathbf{I} & \mathbf{0} \end{pmatrix}. \]

The four blocks have different roles. \(\mathbf{P}\) contains survival-growth transitions from \(t\) to \(t+1\), whereas \(\mathbf{F}\) produces recruits at \(t+1\) from the population at \(t-1\). The identity matrix \(\mathbf{I}\) transfers the current population into the historical position for the next projection, and \(\mathbf{0}\) prevents the stored population from contributing directly to the following state.

Importantly, \(\mathbf{I}\) is only a bookkeeping device. It does not represent a biological demographic transition. Kuss et al. (2008): “simply a computational device and not a biological transition”

8.3.1 Implementation for Polygala lewtonii

In the implementation used here, the survival-growth matrix is called Tmat and corresponds to \(\mathbf{P}\) above, while the fecundity matrix is called Fmat. With disturbance state \(d\), the model is therefore

\[ \mathbf{K}_{\mathrm{lag}}(d) = \begin{pmatrix} \mathbf{T}_d & \mathbf{F}_d \\ \mathbf{I} & \mathbf{0} \end{pmatrix}. \]

For 200 size mesh points, both \(\mathbf{T}_d\) and \(\mathbf{F}_d\) are \(200\times200\) matrices, producing a \(400\times400\) time-lagged megamatrix.

This first implementation deliberately uses a simplified disturbance representation. A single disturbance state \(d\) is supplied to the demographic components when constructing each kernel. The purpose of this model is therefore to isolate the consequences of introducing the one-year fecundity lag and to reproduce the basic megamatrix formulation of Kuss et al. (2008).

The second historical model removes this simplification and explicitly retains the different timing of fire effects among the vital rates.

8.4 Environmental historical IPM

For Polygala lewtonii, the relevant historical dependence arises naturally from the timing of fire relative to the annual census. Let

\[ D_{t-1} \]

denote disturbance during the interval from \(t-1\) to \(t\), and

\[ D_t \]

denote disturbance during the interval from \(t\) to \(t+1\).

Yet again: Ehrlén (2000): “the current phenotype of an individual and its response to environmental change have been shown to reflect the individual’s history, i.e., its past phenotype and environment”

These two disturbance states affect different demographic processes. Survival and growth from \(t\) to \(t+1\) depend on \(D_t\). Recruitment from flowering stems at \(t\) to recruits at \(t+1\) also depends on \(D_t\). In contrast, flowering probability and flowering-stem production observed at \(t\) depend on disturbance during the preceding interval, \(D_{t-1}\).

The demographic kernel for one projection interval must therefore be conditional on both disturbance states. With binary disturbance, \(D\in\{0,1\}\), four kernels are required:

\[ \mathbf{K}_{00},\qquad \mathbf{K}_{01},\qquad \mathbf{K}_{10},\qquad \mathbf{K}_{11}, \]

where the first subscript denotes current disturbance \(D_t\) and the second denotes previous disturbance \(D_{t-1}\).

For example,

\[ \mathbf{K}_{10} \]

describes demographic transitions during a year with current fire \((D_t=1)\) that follows an unburned previous interval \((D_{t-1}=0)\).

Each state-specific kernel can be written as

\[ \mathbf{K}_{ij} = \mathbf{P}_i + \mathbf{F}_{ij}, \]

where

\[ i=D_t,\qquad j=D_{t-1}. \]

The survival-growth component depends only on current disturbance,

\[ P_i(y,x) = s(x\mid D_t=i) \,g(y,x\mid D_t=i), \]

whereas fecundity depends on both disturbance intervals,

\[ F_{ij}(y,x) = r(y)\, b(x\mid D_{t-1}=j,D_t=i). \]

Here, \(r(y)\) describes the recruit-size distribution and \(b(x\mid D_{t-1},D_t)\) represents expected recruitment generated by an individual of size \(x\). In the fitted model, flowering probability and flowering-stem production contribute the dependence on \(D_{t-1}\), whereas the flowering-stem-to-recruit relationship contributes the dependence on \(D_t\).

8.4.1 Carrying the disturbance history forward

The model must also specify how disturbance states themselves change through time. Conditional transition probabilities are estimated from the observed fire histories:

\[ p_{i|j} = P(D_t=i\mid D_{t-1}=j). \]

For the two-state disturbance process,

\[ p_{0|0}+p_{1|0}=1 \]

and

\[ p_{0|1}+p_{1|1}=1. \]

The population at time \(t\) is separated according to the disturbance state experienced during the preceding interval:

\[ \mathbf{N}_t = \begin{pmatrix} \mathbf{n}_t^{(0)} \ \mathbf{n}_t^{(1)} \end{pmatrix}, \]

where

\[ \mathbf{n}_t^{(0)} \]

contains individuals for which \(D_{t-1}=0\), and

\[ \mathbf{n}_t^{(1)} \]

contains individuals for which \(D_{t-1}=1\).

The environmental historical projection is then

\[ \begin{pmatrix} \mathbf{n}_{t+1}^{(0)} \\ \mathbf{n}_{t+1}^{(1)} \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} p_{0|0}\mathbf{K}_{00} & p_{0|1}\mathbf{K}_{01} \\ p_{1|0}\mathbf{K}_{10} & p_{1|1}\mathbf{K}_{11} \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} \mathbf{n}_t^{(0)} \\ \mathbf{n}_t^{(1)} \end{pmatrix}. \]

Thus, the environmental historical megamatrix is

\[ \mathbf{K}_{\mathrm{env}} = \begin{pmatrix} p_{0|0}\mathbf{K}_{00} & p_{0|1}\mathbf{K}_{01} \\ p_{1|0}\mathbf{K}_{10} & p_{1|1}\mathbf{K}_{11} \end{pmatrix}. \]

After projection, the upper block contains individuals whose new previous disturbance state is \(D_t=0\), while the lower block contains individuals whose new previous disturbance state is \(D_t=1\). In this way, the disturbance experienced during one projection becomes the historical disturbance state used in the next.

As in the time-lagged model, 200 size mesh points and two historical states produce a \(400\times400\) megamatrix. However, the interpretation of those 400 states is fundamentally different.

8.5 Time-lagged versus environmental historical IPMs

Both models extend the ordinary IPM by augmenting the population state, but they retain different kinds of information.

In the time-lagged model,

\[ \mathbf{N}_t = \begin{pmatrix} \mathbf{n}_t \\ \mathbf{n}_{t-1} \end{pmatrix}, \]

and the lower half of the state vector is a stored copy of the previous population. The identity block exists solely to carry this information forward. Fecundity is then applied to the lagged population.

In the environmental historical model,

\[ \mathbf{N}_t = \begin{pmatrix} \mathbf{n}_t^{(D_{t-1}=0)} \\ \mathbf{n}_t^{(D_{t-1}=1)} \end{pmatrix}. \]

Here, both halves contain real individuals at time \(t\). They are mutually exclusive components of the current population, distinguished by the environment experienced during the preceding interval. No identity bookkeeping block is required. Instead, conditional disturbance-transition probabilities move individuals between environmental-history states.

The distinction can therefore be summarized as

\[ \text{time-lagged model:} \qquad \text{memory of the population at }t-1, \]

versus

\[ \text{environmental historical model:} \qquad \text{memory of the environment during }t-1\rightarrow t. \]

Neither formulation is identical to a fully individual-history IPM in which vital rates depend directly on both current and previous individual size, such as

\[ z_{t+1} \sim z_t + z_{t-1}. \]

In such models, the individual state is defined by the pair \((z_{t-1},z_t)\), and transitions occur between consecutive state pairs (Ehrlén 2000; Shefferson et al. 2021). The models implemented here instead focus on two specific forms of temporal dependence that are directly relevant to the demographic structure of the Polygala lewtonii IPM.

8.6.1 Load the completed workdata

The workdata already contains current-year disturbance and disturbance in the exact previous year. These fields are retained directly rather than rebuilt from the subset of observed individual rows.

Code 
df <- read.csv(
  file.path(
    dir_data,
    paste0('ab_', v_sp_abb, '_df_workdata_260519.csv'))) %>%
  mutate(
    disturbance = as.numeric(dist_transition),
    disturbance_prev = as.numeric(disturbance_prev),
    year = as.integer(year),
    site = factor(site)) %>%
  filter(
    !is.na(year),
    !(year %in% v_years_re))

8.7 Construct the vital-rate data sets

8.7.1 Survival

Code 
df_su <- df %>%
  filter(
    !is.na(survives),
    size_t0 != 0,
    is.finite(logvol_t0),
    is.finite(logvol_t0_2),
    is.finite(logvol_t0_3),
    !is.na(disturbance)) %>%
  dplyr::select(
    id, site, year, size_t0, survives, size_t1,
    logsize_t0, logsize_t1, logsize_t0_2, logsize_t0_3,
    volume_t0, volume_t1, logvol_t0, logvol_t1,
    logvol_t0_2, logvol_t0_3, disturbance, stage)

8.7.3 Flowering probability and flowering-stem number

Observed recruits are retained because some recruits flowered.

Code 
df_fl <- df %>%
  filter(
    !is.na(flower),
    is.finite(logvol_t0),
    is.finite(logvol_t0_2),
    is.finite(logvol_t0_3),
    !is.na(disturbance_prev)) %>%
  dplyr::select(
    id, site, year, size_t0, flower, fl_nr, size_t1,
    logsize_t0, logsize_t1, logsize_t0_2, logsize_t0_3,
    volume_t0, volume_t1, logvol_t0, logvol_t1,
    logvol_t0_2, logvol_t0_3, disturbance_prev, stage, recruits)

df_fl_cond <- df_fl %>%
  filter(
    flower == 1,
    !is.na(fl_nr),
    fl_nr > 0,
    fl_nr == round(fl_nr))

8.7.4 Quadrat-level flowering stems and recruits

Total flowering stems in quadrat \(q\) during year \(t\) predict recruits in the same quadrat during year \(t+1\). A quadrat transition is retained only when the same quadrat has individual records in both years.

Code 
df_quad_year_sampled <- df %>%
  distinct(site, quad, year)

df_fs2r <- df %>%
  group_by(site, quad, year) %>%
  summarise(
    fs_t0 = sum(fl_nr, na.rm = TRUE),
    disturbance = if_else(
      all(is.na(disturbance)),
      NA_real_,
      max(disturbance, na.rm = TRUE)),
    .groups = 'drop') %>%
  mutate(
    year_t1 = year + 1) %>%
  semi_join(
    df_quad_year_sampled %>%
      transmute(
        site,
        quad,
        year_t1 = year),
    by = c(
      'site',
      'quad',
      'year_t1')) %>%
  left_join(
    df %>%
      filter(recruits == 1) %>%
      count(
        site,
        quad,
        year,
        name = 're_t1'),
    by = c(
      'site',
      'quad',
      'year_t1' = 'year')) %>%
  mutate(
    re_t1 = replace_na(re_t1, 0L),
    site = factor(site),
    fs_t0_log = log1p(fs_t0),
    re_t1_log = log1p(re_t1)) %>%
  filter(
    !is.na(year),
    !is.na(year_t1),
    !is.na(disturbance),
    !(year %in% v_years_re),
    !(year_t1 %in% v_years_re))

df_fs2r %>%
  summarise(
    quadrats = n_distinct(quad),
    transitions = n(),
    zero_stems = sum(fs_t0 == 0),
    zero_recruits = sum(re_t1 == 0),
    burned_transitions = sum(disturbance == 1),
    unburned_transitions = sum(disturbance == 0))

8.8 Fit the mean vital-rate models

Candidate models use intercept-only, fire-only, and first- through third-order size polynomials, each with and without the relevant fire term. Empty model-set vectors select the model with the lowest AICc.

8.8.1 Survival model

Code 
mod_su_00 <- glm(
  survives ~ 1,
  data = df_su,
  family = binomial)

mod_su_0 <- glm(
  survives ~ disturbance,
  data = df_su,
  family = binomial)

mod_su_10 <- glm(
  survives ~ logvol_t0,
  data = df_su,
  family = binomial)

mod_su_1 <- glm(
  survives ~ logvol_t0 + disturbance,
  data = df_su,
  family = binomial)

mod_su_20 <- glm(
  survives ~ logvol_t0 + logvol_t0_2,
  data = df_su,
  family = binomial)

mod_su_2 <- glm(
  survives ~ logvol_t0 + logvol_t0_2 + disturbance,
  data = df_su,
  family = binomial)

mod_su_30 <- glm(
  survives ~ logvol_t0 + logvol_t0_2 + logvol_t0_3,
  data = df_su,
  family = binomial)

mod_su_3 <- glm(
  survives ~ logvol_t0 + logvol_t0_2 + logvol_t0_3 +
    disturbance,
  data = df_su,
  family = binomial)

mods_su <- list(
  mod_su_00, mod_su_0, mod_su_10, mod_su_1,
  mod_su_20, mod_su_2, mod_su_30, mod_su_3)

mods_su_dAICc <- bbmle::AICctab(
  mods_su,
  weights = TRUE,
  sort = FALSE)$dAICc

mods_su_sorted <- order(mods_su_dAICc)

if (length(v_mod_set_su) == 0) {
  mod_su_index_best <- mods_su_sorted[1]
} else {
  mod_su_index_best <- v_mod_set_su + 1
}

v_mod_su_index <- floor((mod_su_index_best - 1) / 2)
mod_su_best <- mods_su[[mod_su_index_best]]

summary(mod_su_best)

8.8.3 Growth variance

Growth variance is modeled as an exponential function of the fitted growth mean.

Code 
mod_gr_x <- fitted(mod_gr_best)
mod_gr_y <- resid(mod_gr_best)^2

mod_gr_var <- nls(
  mod_gr_y ~ a * exp(b * mod_gr_x),
  start = list(a = 1, b = 0),
  control = nls.control(
    maxiter = 1000,
    tol = 1e-6,
    warnOnly = TRUE))

summary(mod_gr_var)

8.8.6 Flowering-stem-to-recruit model

The recruitment candidates allow a seedbank intercept, a current-fire effect, a flowering-stem effect, and their interaction. No year or site random effects are fitted.

Code 
mod_re_00 <- lm(
  re_t1_log ~ 1,
  data = df_fs2r)

mod_re_0 <- lm(
  re_t1_log ~ disturbance,
  data = df_fs2r)

mod_re_10 <- lm(
  re_t1_log ~ fs_t0_log,
  data = df_fs2r)

mod_re_1 <- lm(
  re_t1_log ~ fs_t0_log + disturbance,
  data = df_fs2r)

mod_re_20 <- lm(
  re_t1_log ~ fs_t0_log * disturbance,
  data = df_fs2r)

mods_re <- list(
  mod_re_00,
  mod_re_0,
  mod_re_10,
  mod_re_1,
  mod_re_20)

mods_re_dAICc <- bbmle::AICctab(
  mods_re,
  weights = TRUE,
  sort = FALSE)$dAICc

mods_re_sorted <- order(mods_re_dAICc)

if (length(v_mod_set_re) == 0) {
  mod_re_index_best <- mods_re_sorted[1]
} else {
  mod_re_index_best <- v_mod_set_re + 1
}

v_mod_re_index <- mod_re_index_best - 1
mod_re_best <- mods_re[[mod_re_index_best]]

8.8.7 Recruitment-model support

Code 
df_recruit_model_support <- tibble(
  model = c(
    'Intercept only',
    'Disturbance only',
    'Flowering stems',
    'Flowering stems + disturbance',
    'Full interaction'),
  dAICc = as.numeric(mods_re_dAICc)) %>%
  mutate(
    weight = exp(-0.5 * dAICc) /
      sum(exp(-0.5 * dAICc))) %>%
  arrange(dAICc)

knitr::kable(
  df_recruit_model_support,
  digits = c(NA, 2, 3),
  caption = paste(
    'AICc support for quadrat-level flowering-stem-to-recruit',
    'models.'))
(#tab:unnamed-chunk-23)AICc support for quadrat-level flowering-stem-to-recruit models.
model dAICc weight
Full interaction 0.00 0.569
Disturbance only 1.56 0.260
Flowering stems + disturbance 2.40 0.171
Intercept only 52.77 0.000
Flowering stems 53.63 0.000

The full interaction model is selected. Its fitted form is

\[ \log(1 + R_{q,t+1}) = \beta_0 + \beta_1\log(1 + M_{q,t}) + \beta_d d_{q,t} + \beta_{1d}\log(1 + M_{q,t})d_{q,t} + \varepsilon, \]

where \(M_{q,t}\) is total flowering stems, \(R_{q,t+1}\) is the number of recruits in the same quadrat in the following year, and \(d_{q,t}\) indicates current fire.

8.8.8 Recruitment slopes and uncertainty

Code 
re_coef <- coef(mod_re_20)
re_vcov <- vcov(mod_re_20)

slope_unburned <- re_coef['fs_t0_log']

se_unburned <- sqrt(
  re_vcov[
    'fs_t0_log',
    'fs_t0_log'])

slope_burned <-
  re_coef['fs_t0_log'] +
  re_coef['fs_t0_log:disturbance']

se_burned <- sqrt(
  re_vcov[
    'fs_t0_log',
    'fs_t0_log'] +
  re_vcov[
    'fs_t0_log:disturbance',
    'fs_t0_log:disturbance'] +
  2 * re_vcov[
    'fs_t0_log',
    'fs_t0_log:disturbance'])

df_recruit_slopes <- tibble(
  disturbance = c(0, 1),
  slope = c(
    slope_unburned,
    slope_burned),
  lower_95 = c(
    slope_unburned - 1.96 * se_unburned,
    slope_burned - 1.96 * se_burned),
  upper_95 = c(
    slope_unburned + 1.96 * se_unburned,
    slope_burned + 1.96 * se_burned))

knitr::kable(
  df_recruit_slopes,
  digits = 3,

8.9 Plot the selected vital-rate models

Code 
make_mean_prediction <- function(data, model, disturbance_var) {
  x <- seq(
    min(data$logvol_t0, na.rm = TRUE),
    max(data$logvol_t0, na.rm = TRUE),
    length.out = 200)

  pred <- expand_grid(
    logvol_t0 = x,
    disturbance_value = c(0, 1)) %>%
    mutate(
      logvol_t0_2 = logvol_t0^2,
      logvol_t0_3 = logvol_t0^3,
      disturbance_plot = factor(
        disturbance_value,
        levels = c(0, 1),
        labels = c('No fire', 'Fire')))

  pred[[disturbance_var]] <- pred$disturbance_value
  pred$prediction <- predict(
    model,
    newdata = pred,
    type = 'response')

  pred
}

make_mean_plot <- function(
    data, model, response, disturbance_var, title, y_lab,
    probability = FALSE) {
  pred <- make_mean_prediction(
    data = data,
    model = model,
    disturbance_var = disturbance_var)

  data_plot <- data %>%
    mutate(
      disturbance_plot = factor(
        .data[[disturbance_var]],
        levels = c(0, 1),
        labels = c('No fire', 'Fire')))

  point_layer <- if (probability) {
    geom_jitter(
      data = data_plot,
      aes(
        x = logvol_t0,
        y = .data[[response]],
        color = disturbance_plot),
      alpha = 0.15,
      size = 0.7,
      width = 0.05,
      height = 0.05)
  } else {
    geom_point(
      data = data_plot,
      aes(
        x = logvol_t0,
        y = .data[[response]],
        color = disturbance_plot),
      alpha = 0.15,
      size = 0.7)
  }

  p <- ggplot() +
    point_layer +
    geom_line(
      data = pred,
      aes(
        x = logvol_t0,
        y = prediction,
        color = disturbance_plot),
      linewidth = 0.8) +
    scale_color_manual(
      values = c(
        'No fire' = 'black',
        'Fire' = 'red')) +
    theme_bw() +
    labs(
      title = title,
      subtitle = v_ggp_suffix,
      x = expression('log(volume)'[t0]),
      y = y_lab,
      color = NULL)

  if (probability) {
    p <- p + coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, 1))
  }

  p
}

8.11 Extract the selected model parameters

The extraction functions return zero for terms that are absent from the selected model. The same IPM functions can therefore use any selected candidate without manual coefficient changes.

Code 
size_term_map <- c(
  b0 = '(Intercept)',
  b1 = 'logvol_t0',
  b2 = 'logvol_t0_2',
  b3 = 'logvol_t0_3',
  bd = 'disturbance')

lagged_size_term_map <- c(
  b0 = '(Intercept)',
  b1 = 'logvol_t0',
  b2 = 'logvol_t0_2',
  b3 = 'logvol_t0_3',
  bd = 'disturbance_prev')

extract_terms <- function(model, prefix, term_map) {
  coefs <- stats::coef(model)

  values <- vapply(term_map, function(term_i) {
    if (term_i %in% names(coefs)) {
      unname(coefs[[term_i]])
    } else {
      0
    }
  }, numeric(1))

  names(values) <- paste0(prefix, names(term_map))
  values
}

extract_coef <- function(model, term, default = 0) {
  coefs <- stats::coef(model)

  if (term %in% names(coefs)) {
    unname(coefs[[term]])
  } else {
    default
  }
}

grow_var_coef <- stats::coef(mod_gr_var)

mesh_limits <- range(
  c(
    df_gr$logvol_t0,
    df_gr$logvol_t1,
    df_recr$logvol_t0),
  na.rm = TRUE,
  finite = TRUE)

mesh_limits <- c(
  mesh_limits[1] - 0.1,
  mesh_limits[2] + 0.1)

pars_mean <- as.list(c(
  extract_terms(
    mod_su_best,
    'surv_',
    size_term_map),
  extract_terms(
    mod_gr_best,
    'grow_',
    size_term_map),
  extract_terms(
    mod_fl_best,
    'fl_',
    lagged_size_term_map),
  extract_terms(
    mod_fl_n_best,
    'fln_',
    lagged_size_term_map),
  re_b0 = extract_coef(
    mod_re_best,
    '(Intercept)'),
  re_b1 = extract_coef(
    mod_re_best,
    'fs_t0_log'),
  re_bd = extract_coef(
    mod_re_best,
    'disturbance'),
  re_bf = extract_coef(
    mod_re_best,
    'fs_t0_log:disturbance'),
  re_sigma = stats::sigma(mod_re_best),
  recr_mean = rc_sz$mean,
  recr_sd = rc_sz$sd,
  grow_var_a = unname(grow_var_coef[['a']]),
  grow_var_b = unname(grow_var_coef[['b']]),
  fs_ref = mean(df_fs2r$fs_t0, na.rm = TRUE),
  L = mesh_limits[1],
  U = mesh_limits[2],
  mat_siz = 200,
  mod_su_index = v_mod_su_index,
  mod_gr_index = v_mod_gr_index,
  mod_fl_index = v_mod_fl_index,
  mod_fl_n_index = v_mod_fl_n_index,
  mod_re_index = v_mod_re_index))

pars_mean_table <- tibble(
  parameter = names(pars_mean),

8.12 Define the IPM functions

The extracted flowering coefficients still come from models fitted with disturbance_prev. From this point onward, however, their disturbance coefficient is used with the same generic disturbance argument as all other vital rates.

8.12.1 General parameter and linear-predictor functions

Code 
get_par <- function(pars, par_name, default = 0) {
  if (!is.null(pars[[par_name]])) {
    pars[[par_name]]
  } else {
    default
  }
}

vital_lp <- function(x, pars, prefix, disturbance = 0) {
  get_par(pars, paste0(prefix, 'b0')) +
    get_par(pars, paste0(prefix, 'b1')) * x +
    get_par(pars, paste0(prefix, 'b2')) * x^2 +
    get_par(pars, paste0(prefix, 'b3')) * x^3 +
    get_par(pars, paste0(prefix, 'bd')) * disturbance
}

###Survival

Code 
sx <- function(x, pars, disturbance = 0) {
  plogis(vital_lp(
    x = x,
    pars = pars,
    prefix = 'surv_',
    disturbance = disturbance))
}

###Growth

Code 
grow_mu <- function(x, pars, disturbance = 0) {
  vital_lp(
    x = x,
    pars = pars,
    prefix = 'grow_',
    disturbance = disturbance)
}

grow_sd <- function(mean_value, pars) {
  variance <- get_par(pars, 'grow_var_a') *
    exp(get_par(pars, 'grow_var_b') * mean_value)

  sqrt(pmax(variance, .Machine$double.eps))
}

gxy <- function(x, y, pars, disturbance = 0) {
  mean_value <- grow_mu(
    x = x,
    pars = pars,
    disturbance = disturbance)

  sd_value <- grow_sd(
    mean_value = mean_value,
    pars = pars)

  dnorm(y, mean = mean_value, sd = sd_value)
}

8.12.2 Flowering probability and flowering-stem number

For this initial Kuss-style implementation, disturbance is intentionally treated as a single common state within the IPM. Although the flowering models were fitted using disturbance_prev, their extracted disturbance coefficients are evaluated using the same generic disturbance state used for the other vital rates.

This is a simplifying assumption used to implement and examine the time-lagged matrix structure. It does not yet reproduce the actual difference in fire timing among the vital rates.

Code 
fl_x <- function(x, pars, disturbance = 0) {
  plogis(vital_lp(
    x = x,
    pars = pars,
    prefix = 'fl_',
    disturbance = disturbance))
}

fln_x <- function(x, pars, disturbance = 0) {
  exp(vital_lp(
    x = x,
    pars = pars,
    prefix = 'fln_',
    disturbance = disturbance))
}

fs_x <- function(x, pars, disturbance = 0) {
  fl_x(
    x = x,
    pars = pars,
    disturbance = disturbance) *
    fln_x(
      x = x,
      pars = pars,
      disturbance = disturbance)
}

###Recruitment

Code 
predict_recruits_from_stems <- function(
    flowering_stems, pars, disturbance = 0) {
  stems_nonnegative <- pmax(flowering_stems, 0)

  slope <- get_par(pars, 're_b1') +
    get_par(pars, 're_bf') * disturbance

  eta <- get_par(pars, 're_b0') +
    get_par(pars, 're_bd') * disturbance +
    slope * log1p(stems_nonnegative)

  recruits <- expm1(
    eta + 0.5 * get_par(pars, 're_sigma')^2)

  pmax(recruits, 0)
}

recruits_per_stem <- function(pars, disturbance = 0) {
  fs_ref <- get_par(pars, 'fs_ref', 0)

  if (!is.finite(fs_ref) || fs_ref <= 0) {
    return(0)
  }

  predict_recruits_from_stems(
    flowering_stems = fs_ref,
    pars = pars,
    disturbance = disturbance) / fs_ref
}

rx <- function(x, pars, disturbance = 0) {
  fs_x(
    x = x,
    pars = pars,
    disturbance = disturbance) *
    recruits_per_stem(
      pars = pars,
      disturbance = disturbance)
}

recr_y <- function(y, pars) {
  dnorm(
    y,
    mean = get_par(pars, 'recr_mean'),
    sd = get_par(pars, 'recr_sd'))
}

fy <- function(y, x, pars, h, disturbance = 0) {
  Pvec <- recr_y(y, pars)
  recruit_mass <- sum(Pvec * h)

  if (!is.finite(recruit_mass) || recruit_mass <= 0) {
    stop('Recruit size distribution has no mass inside the mesh')
  }

  Pvec <- Pvec / recruit_mass

  Rvec <- rx(
    x = x,
    pars = pars,
    disturbance = disturbance)

  outer(Pvec, Rvec) * h
}

8.13 Construct the time-lagged IPM

The standard mean IPM combines the survival-growth and fecundity matrices within a single projection matrix,

\[ \mathbf{K} = \mathbf{P} + \mathbf{F}. \]

In the code below, Tmat corresponds to the survival-growth matrix \(\mathbf{P}\) of Kuss et al. (2008). For comparison with the original ahistorical model, k_yx retains the standard matrix

\[ \mathbf{K} = \mathbf{P} + \mathbf{F}. \]

The historical model instead places survival-growth and fecundity in different blocks of a larger projection matrix:

\[ \mathbf{K}_H = \begin{pmatrix} \mathbf{P} & \mathbf{F} \\ \mathbf{I} & \mathbf{0} \end{pmatrix}. \]

With 200 mesh points, the ordinary IPM is a \(200 \times 200\) matrix, whereas the historical IPM is a \(400 \times 400\) matrix.

Code 
kernel <- function(pars, disturbance = 0) {
  n <- as.integer(pars$mat_siz)
  L <- pars$L
  U <- pars$U
  h <- (U - L) / n

  b <- L + c(0:n) * h
  y <- 0.5 * (b[1:n] + b[2:(n + 1)])

  Fmat <- fy(
    y = y,
    x = y,
    pars = pars,
    h = h,
    disturbance = disturbance)

  Smat <- sx(
    x = y,
    pars = pars,
    disturbance = disturbance)

  Gmat <- matrix(0, n, n)
  Gmat[] <- t(
    outer(
      y,
      y,
      Vectorize(function(x, y) {
        gxy(
          x = x,
          y = y,
          pars = pars,
          disturbance = disturbance)
      }))) * h

  Tmat <- matrix(0, n, n)

  for (i in 1:(n / 2)) {
    Gmat[1, i] <- Gmat[1, i] + 1 - sum(Gmat[, i])
    Tmat[, i] <- Gmat[, i] * Smat[i]
  }

  for (i in (n / 2 + 1):n) {
    Gmat[n, i] <- Gmat[n, i] + 1 - sum(Gmat[, i])
    Tmat[, i] <- Gmat[, i] * Smat[i]
  }

  k_yx <- Fmat + Tmat

  Imat <- diag(n)
  Zmat <- matrix(0, n, n)

  K_hist <- rbind(
    cbind(Tmat, Fmat),
    cbind(Imat, Zmat))

  list(
    k_yx = k_yx,
    K_hist = K_hist,
    Fmat = Fmat,
    Tmat = Tmat,
    Imat = Imat,
    Zmat = Zmat,
    Gmat = Gmat,
    Smat = Smat,
    meshpts = y,
    h = h)
}

The lower-left identity matrix is not a demographic transition. It is a bookkeeping operator that transfers the current population vector into the historical component of the state vector for the following projection (Kuss et al. 2008).

##Historical asymptotic population growth rate

Population growth is calculated from the dominant eigenvalue of the full historical megamatrix rather than from the ordinary \(\mathbf{P}+\mathbf{F}\) matrix.

Code 
lambda_ipm <- function(pars, disturbance = 0) {
  K <- kernel(
    pars = pars,
    disturbance = disturbance)$K_hist

  Re(eigen(K, only.values = TRUE)$values[1])
}

##Observed structures ### Mean observed size distribution

Code 
make_initial_n_mean <- function(pars, df_init = df) {
  n <- as.integer(pars$mat_siz)
  L <- pars$L
  U <- pars$U
  h <- (U - L) / n
  breaks <- seq(L, U, length.out = n + 1)
  b <- L + c(0:n) * h
  y <- 0.5 * (b[1:n] + b[2:(n + 1)])
  
  recruit_density <- recr_y(y, pars)
  recruit_density <- recruit_density / sum(recruit_density * h)
  
  years_i <- df_init %>%
    filter(!is.na(year)) %>%
    distinct(year) %>%
    arrange(year) %>%
    pull(year)
  
  counts_by_year <- purrr::map(years_i, function(year_i) {
    df_i <- df_init %>%
      filter(year == year_i)
    
    x <- df_i %>%
      filter(is.finite(logvol_t0)) %>%
      pull(logvol_t0)
    
    size_counts <- hist(
      pmin(pmax(x, L), U),
      breaks = breaks,
      plot = FALSE,
      include.lowest = TRUE)$counts
    
    n_unsized_recruits <- df_i %>%
      summarise(
        n = sum(
          !is.finite(logvol_t0) & recruits == 1,
          na.rm = TRUE)) %>%
      pull(n)
    
    size_counts + n_unsized_recruits * recruit_density * h
  })
  
  mean_counts <- Reduce(`+`, counts_by_year) / length(counts_by_year)
  mean_counts / h
}
